blocks.text: This thesis examines whether explainable machine learning can make financial forecasting more trustworthy. It considers accuracy, interpretability, stability over time, faithfulness and economic meaning separately. Seven models: Linear Regression, ARIMA, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, LSTM and a simplified Temporal Fusion Transformer are tested on four financial indices and the Monash Sunspot series.

Experiments use four lagged predictors, one- and five-step horizons and rolling and expanding walk-forward evaluation. Comparisons cover 18,480 matched origins, with Diebold–Mariano tests adjusted for multiple comparisons within each setting.

Across 16 financial settings, no model beats persistence on average and every model has negative mean R². Linear Regression has nine significant pairwise wins and no significant losses, Random Forest has no wins and 15 significant losses. Another 224 financial tests using each model’s full forecast coverage find no significant improvement over persistence or the average training target. The results do not show that black-box models consistently outperform simpler models or that post-hoc explanations resolve the accuracy – interpretability trade-off.

For all models, explanations from one-fold to the next usually agree more closely under expanding windows than under rolling windows, but some cases still have low stability. Stability depends on the model, explanation method, evaluation scheme, and market regime, with no consistent decline during bear or crisis markets. For the relevant methods, the explanation parts add up to the predictions apart from small numerical errors. Other checks give mixed evidence about faithfulness. In this thesis, lag-based explanations cannot show cause-and-effect economic relationships.
Post-hoc explanations can help inspect models, but they do not guarantee accurate forecasts, stable or faithful explanations, or valid economic conclusions.
Keywords
Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Financial Time-Series Forecasting, Interpretable Machine Learning, SHAP, LIME, Temporal Stability, Faithfulness.
Background and Motivation
Machine Learning in Financial Forecasting

Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) now have a central role in quantitative financial research. Gradient-boosted trees, random forests, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and transformer-based architectures are increasingly used for tasks that were once dominated by linear econometric models. These tasks include return prediction, risk-premium measurement, volatility forecasting, and trading-signal generation.

The main empirical motivation is the ability of flexible models to represent nonlinear relationships. In a large study of equity risk premia, Gu et al. (2020) report that tree-based methods and neural networks provide the best out-of-sample predictive and portfolio performance. They attribute much of this gain to nonlinear predictor interactions that linear specifications do not capture. Fischer and Krauss (2018) provide a related example. Their LSTM networks outperformed a random forest, a deep neural network, and logistic regression in out-of-sample directional prediction of S&P 500 constituents from 1992 to 2015. The study also reported strong risk-adjusted returns before transaction costs.

These results, however, sit within a longer and more cautious research record. Financial prediction is difficult because markets are noisy and, in the generally accepted semi-strong form, incorporate publicly available information into prices (Fischer & Krauss, 2018, p. 654). (Tsay, 2005, pp. 180–183) showed that carefully tuned feed-forward neural networks did not systematically outperform a random walk with drift when forecasting monthly IBM log prices. Forecast errors also varied substantially when the same network was re-estimated.

Later comparisons have reached similarly qualified conclusions. (Molnar, 2022, pp. 57–58) notes that classical statistical models have often been competitive with, or superior to, ML models in systematic time series comparisons. This applies to comparisons involving LSTM networks and multi-layer neural networks as well. Even the results of Fischer and Krauss (2018) have a temporal qualification: the reported LSTM excess returns were concentrated in the earlier sample period and appeared to have largely disappeared from 2010 onward. Flexible models can therefore extract predictive signal, but their advantage may vary across periods and cannot be assumed in advance.

Benchmarking resources have developed alongside these models. The Monash Time Series Forecasting Archive introduced standardized multi-dataset evaluation across domains (Godahewa et al., 2021). FinTSB more recently systematized financial forecasting evaluation, with attention to temporal leakage, non-stationarity, regime diversity, and market frictions (Hu et al., 2026). These resources support more rigorous comparisons of predictive performance. They do not, by themselves, establish whether the resulting models are interpretable or whether their explanations are dependable.
The Black-Box Problem and the Regulatory Context

The flexibility of complex models also makes them difficult to inspect. A black-box model has an internal structure that humans cannot readily comprehend directly. A glass-box model, in contrast, has a mechanism that can in principle be understood through inspection (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, pp. 8–10). Random forests, gradient-boosting ensembles, LSTMs, and the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) fall on the black-box side of this distinction. Gu et al.(2020) also identify deep neural networks as among the least transparent methods used in empirical asset pricing. (Green, 2026, para. 1.4) takes a more qualified view but still describes deep networks as, at best, “grey boxes” whose learned features require exploration.

Opacity would be less concerning if predictive accuracy were the only relevant criterion. (James et al., 2013, pp. 24–26) explain that interpretability generally decreases as flexibility increases. A researcher might therefore choose the most flexible model for stock-price prediction. Yet the same authors caution that less flexible methods can be more accurate because highly flexible methods are vulnerable to overfitting.

Financial practice introduces further requirements. Decisions can involve substantial monetary risk, fiduciary duties, and strict regulatory frameworks. In high-stakes applications, opaque AI systems may create legal, ethical, and financial risks, including regulatory penalties and loss of stakeholder trust (Hoang et al., 2026, p. 193). In credit modeling, interpretability may even constitute a legal requirement (Hull, 2021, p. 135). MiFID II governance and auditability expectations for algorithmic trading, together with the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act), have also increased attention to transparency and traceability. Explainability methods are discussed as one response to these demands (Von Zahn et al., 2025).

Explanations also affect the people who use model outputs. Experimental evidence reported by von Zahn et al. (2025) indicates that explanations can improve users’ metaknowledge: the alignment between their confidence and their actual performance. This improvement can support better decisions about when to delegate a task to an AI system. The value of an explanation therefore depends not only on its visual appeal but also on whether it represents the model reliably.

Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offers two main responses to the black-box problem (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, p. 7; Molnar, 2022, p. 3). The first is to use an intrinsically interpretable model, such as a linear model, a rule-based system, or a small decision tree. Its transparency follows from its structure, although this choice may reduce predictive performance (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, p. 7 see Section 2.3.2).

The second response is to retain a black-box model and apply a post-hoc explanation method. Examples include SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), permutation feature importance, partial dependence, accumulated local effects (ALE), counterfactual explanations, and gradient-based attribution. Native signals such as global feature importance and attention weights can provide additional diagnostic information (Molnar, 2022, pp. 12–13; Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:3–265:4). This thesis uses SHAP and LIME as established examples of the post-hoc toolbox, not as an exhaustive definition of XAI. Its central concern is whether these methods provide dependable transparency for financial time series models or merely create the appearance of transparency.
Properties of Financial Time Series

Several properties of financial time series make both forecasting and explanation difficult. The first is a low signal-to-noise ratio. Daily returns have a mean close to zero and, at most, weak low-order serial correlation. Their predictable component is therefore small relative to their innovation variance (Tsay, 2005, pp. 19–99). In the illustrative S&P 500 analysis of James et al. (2013, pp. 4–5), yesterday’s market movement offers no simple strategy for predicting today’s return. Even a moderately successful classifier achieves only about 60 percent directional accuracy. Under these conditions, spurious strategies can accumulate, and the precision of an individual discovery test is limited (López De Prado, 2020a, p. 106).

Second, financial time series are non-stationary. Strict stationarity means that the joint distribution does not change over time. Weak stationarity instead requires time-invariant mean and autocovariance structures. These concepts underpin much of classical time series analysis and justify using past observations to learn about future observations (Tsay, 2005, p. 25). Asset price levels commonly have a unit root: price has no fixed long-run level, and shocks can have permanent effects. Empirical work therefore often uses transformed series such as log returns,
rt=lnPt-lnPt-1

where Pt is the asset price at time t and rt is the corresponding log return (Tsay, 2005, p. 64). Transformation does not remove all temporal dependence. Financial series still experience bull and bear markets, crisis episodes, structural breaks, and changes in market microstructure. These changes conflict with the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption used in many ML evaluation procedures. Benchmarks that address this problem characterize datasets through unit-root tests and explicitly select series with pronounced non-stationarity (Hu et al., 2026).

Third, financial returns exhibit conditional heteroscedasticity. Volatility changes over time and occurs in clusters. It can remain high in some periods and low in others, evolve continuously rather than only through jumps, and respond asymmetrically to positive and negative shocks. The last pattern is known as the leverage effect (Tsay, 2005, pp. 98–99). Return distributions are also heavy-tailed and have high excess kurtosis relative to the normal distribution (Tsay, 2005, p. 19).

These properties weaken the assumption that relationships learned in one period will remain unchanged in another. The same qualification applies to explanations. An attribution estimated in one volatility regime need not describe model behavior in a different regime. Evaluation procedures designed for static i.i.d. data may not reveal this failure.
Overfitting and Transparency

Overfitting occurs when a flexible model learns noise alongside signal. Because noise is unpredictable by definition, this behavior reduces the reliability of forecasts on new data (López De Prado, 2020a, pp. 7–8). Polynomial classifiers can overfit noisy observations, and neural networks can do so as their capacity increases (Kubat, 2015). Overfitting can affect the training sample directly. It can also affect the test sample when repeated evaluation and selection create selection bias under multiple testing. Strategies may then appear replicable in backtests but fail in implementation (López De Prado, 2020a, pp. 8–9, 105). This concern motivates the broader warning that many published empirical-finance discoveries may be false (López de Prado, 2018; López De Prado, 2020a, p. 8).

Interpretability alone does not prevent overfitting. Intrinsically interpretable models can also fit noise. Single decision trees are easy to visualize but can be unstable under small changes in the training data (Chan et al., 2022, Chapter 2). Conversely, a heavily regularized black-box model may generalize well. The relevant distinction is therefore not that black-box models always overfit more. It is that their failures are harder to inspect when they learn spurious correlations, exploit leakage, or fail under a new market regime.

When a model’s internal structure is complex, analysts may not know which features influence its decisions or how large those influences are. This makes it difficult to assess whether model behavior is consistent with domain knowledge (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, pp. 8–10). Post-hoc explanations promise to improve this transparency and traceability, not to protect against overfitting itself. Whether they fulfill that promise under financial conditions is an empirical question addressed in this thesis.
Problem Statement

ML and DL methods have improved predictive performance in stock-price forecasting and related financial tasks (Fischer & Krauss, 2018; Gu et al., 2020). However, prominent model classes such as gradient boosting, random forests, LSTM networks, and transformers remain difficult for humans to comprehend directly (Molnar, 2022; Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, pp. 8–10). In financial settings, this opacity creates operational risks and complicates governance under frameworks such as MiFID II and the EU AI Act (Hoang et al., 2026, p. 193; Von Zahn et al., 2025).

The statistical environment intensifies the problem. Low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and heteroscedasticity allow flexible models to learn spurious historical relationships or lose accuracy when market conditions change (Tsay, 2005; López de Prado, 2018; 2020a, pp. 7–9). An intrinsically interpretable model at least allows some of these failures to be inspected. A black-box model conceals them unless a separate explanation procedure is applied.

Post-hoc methods do not automatically resolve this difficulty. Many were developed for static i.i.d. settings, and their outputs are not inherently faithful to the model being explained (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:19). Practitioners therefore face a difficult choice. They can accept the possible performance cost of an intrinsically interpretable model, or use a black-box model whose explanations may be unstable, unfaithful, or economically misleading (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, p. 7).

This thesis addresses that choice through a systematic experimental evaluation. It defines trustworthy forecasting as the combination of predictive accuracy with explanations that are understandable, temporally robust, and empirically evaluated for faithfulness. The aim is not to declare one model universally superior. It is to determine what evidence the executed models and explanation methods provide for each dimension of trustworthiness.
Research Gap

Financial forecasting and XAI have developed substantially, but their evaluation practices remain fragmented. Forecasting studies often prioritize predictive performance and give less attention to interpretability (Fischer & Krauss, 2018; Gu et al., 2020). General XAI research focuses more heavily on method development, usually outside the specific statistical conditions of financial time series (Molnar, 2022; Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021). A recent survey finds few rigorous tests of explanation faithfulness and reliability in financial time series forecasting. It also identifies a lack of shared benchmarks and quantitative interpretability metrics (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:30). Three gaps follow from this literature.

Gap 1: Limited integration of predictive and explanation evaluation in finance. Predictive performance and interpretability are commonly assessed separately. Financial forecasting benchmarks increasingly address leakage and realistic market conditions but do not necessarily combine these protocols with systematic XAI evaluation (Hu et al., 2026). At the same time, explanation-quality criteria such as fidelity, stability, comprehensibility, accuracy, and completeness remain difficult to quantify (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:24). No standardized framework covers explanation fidelity, temporal stability under regime shifts, and computational overhead in financial forecasting.

Gap 2: Limited evidence on temporal instability and regime shifts. Financial time series are non-stationary, heteroscedastic, and subject to structural breaks (Tsay, 2005, pp. 64, 98–99). XAI evaluation practice nevertheless relies heavily on static settings and i.i.d. assumptions (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021). Evidence is limited on whether explanations from LSTMs and transformers remain consistent across bull and bear markets, high- and low-volatility periods, and crises. Applied observations suggest that attribution magnitudes can drift even when broad rankings appear stable (Fourné, 2026, p. 44).

Gap 3: Insufficient separation of model faithfulness and economic reliability. In noisy financial markets, ML models can learn spurious, data-mined relationships (López de Prado, 2018; 2020a, p. 106). A mathematically coherent explanation can therefore describe an economically meaningless relationship. Improved predictions do not, on their own, identify economic mechanisms (Gu et al., 2020, p. 2229 see Section 3.2.2). Most interpretability methods describe the model rather than the external world (Molnar, 2022, pp. 28–29).
Research Objectives and Research Questions

The main objective is to evaluate how well explainable ML approaches address predictive accuracy and explanation quality jointly in financial time series forecasting. The study compares intrinsically interpretable models with black-box models supplemented by post-hoc explanations. It has three specific objectives: to quantify the accuracy – interpretability trade-off under walk-forward evaluation with explicit temporal separation, to measure the temporal stability of feature attributions across market regimes, and to assess explanation faithfulness and economic plausibility. These objectives lead to three research questions.
RQ1 (Accuracy – Interpretability Trade-off and Post-hoc Explanations)

In financial time series forecasting, to what extent do post-hoc explanation methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME) mitigate the accuracy – interpretability trade-off between intrinsically interpretable models and black-box architectures (e.g., LSTMs, Temporal Fusion Transformers)?
RQ2 (Temporal Stability & Market Regime Robustness)

To what extent are feature attributions from post-hoc XAI methods temporally stable and robust to non-stationarity, structural breaks, and regime shifts (e.g., bull vs. bear markets, crisis periods) in financial time series?
RQ3 (Faithfulness & Financial Reliability)
To what extent are post-hoc explanations faithful to underlying model mechanics, and do they capture genuine economic drivers rather than spurious correlations?

The questions form a connected sequence. RQ1 asks whether explanations can recover some of the transparency given up when moving toward more flexible models. RQ2 asks whether those explanations remain dependable under the temporal conditions characteristic of financial data. RQ3 asks whether they faithfully represent the model and whether they reveal genuine economic mechanisms. Each question has a corresponding component in the experimental design, results, discussion, and conclusion.
Scope and Delimitation

The executed study is narrower than the initial proposal, and this thesis follows the implementation rather than the planned breadth. The primary domain is daily forecasting for four market indices: the S&P 500, DAX, NASDAQ Composite, and Dow Jones Industrial Average. The executed robustness block contains one daily Sunspot series from the supplied Monash-related materials. Forecast horizons are one and five sessions for the financial series and one and five days for Sunspot. Weekly, monthly, yearly, high-frequency, options, constituent-level, and additional benchmark experiments are outside the executed scope.

The forecasting task uses four lagged predictors: lag_1, lag_5, lag_21, and lag_252. Financial targets are cumulative future log returns, while the Sunspot target is the native future value. No macroeconomic, liquidity, rolling-volatility, drawdown, or other exogenous predictors entered the executed models. The model set is fixed to Linear Regression, ARIMA, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, LSTM, and a simplified Temporal Fusion Transformer adapter. GARCH and other econometric models remain theoretical background only.

The XAI scope comprises exact linear attributions, TreeSHAP, KernelSHAP, a LIME-style local ridge surrogate, permutation feature importance, accumulated local effects where exported, deletion/insertion diagnostics, native ARIMA parameters, and simplified TFT variable-selection and attention signals. These procedures support model-specific diagnostics. They do not provide a comprehensive human-factors, regulatory-compliance, fairness, or causal evaluation. Broader questions of AI governance are discussed only as motivation for reliable explanations.

Several implementation boundaries remain part of the study’s scope. Native deep-model forecasts have shorter sequence-constructed test windows than static forecasts, so primary seven-way comparisons use common origins. ARIMA and the tabular models retain different information sets, explanation coverage is structured rather than exhaustive, and the regime labels are ex post descriptive strata. The earlier ARIMA alignment, deep-probe, intervention-control, and Sunspot-provenance defects were corrected for the present authorized execution and are documented in Appendix D. Lag-only predictors, asymmetric seed replication, and simplified native TFT signals continue to restrict inference, these limitations are reported explicitly rather than removed by re-execution.
Scientific Contributions

This thesis makes four contributions within the preserved experimental scope. First, it provides a fully re-executed, observation-level comparison of seven forecasting models on four financial indices and one non-financial benchmark. Each model exports its forecast origin, target date, realized target, prediction, and benchmark predictions. The main comparison uses only origins shared by all seven models. This avoids rankings based on unequal static and deep test periods.

Second, the study evaluates explanations through separate, reproducible tests instead of relying on visually plausible attribution plots. Linear Regression uses exact linear attributions, and ARIMA uses native selected-lag counterfactuals. The tree ensembles explain the complete two-seed predictor by averaging TreeSHAP values and expected values. The neural models use KernelSHAP on contiguous sequences, followed by signed aggregation over time positions. Stability is measured at identical probe origins across consecutive folds. Where applicable, faithfulness is examined through additivity, permutation importance, deletion/insertion, and a weighted local ridge surrogate. These diagnostics are reported separately because agreement between two methods does not prove that either method is correct.

Third, the thesis includes a detailed correction and provenance record. The corrections cover observation-level statistical testing, ARIMA raw-row alignment and supervised-target benchmarks, deep forecast-origin alignment, contiguous explanation sequences, comparable deep intervention controls, full-ensemble tree explanations, and actual neural SHAP additivity residuals. For the rerun, the supplied Monash CSV replaces the previously unresolved Sunspot input. All 11,109 aligned values are verified against the original TSF. The untraceable normalized input is excluded rather than assumed to be equivalent. Input hashes, package versions, execution times, completion audits, and output checksums accompany the notebooks.

Fourth, the thesis separates statistical attribution from economic identification. The four lag variables can reveal how a fitted predictor uses recent, weekly, monthly, and annual information, but they cannot by themselves identify monetary policy, earnings expectations, liquidity, risk premia, investor sentiment, or other causal economic mechanisms. The economic component of RQ3 is therefore answered through an identification boundary: the study can test model-mechanistic faithfulness, but it cannot certify that the resulting attributions represent genuine economic drivers rather than spurious or merely predictive associations.
Structure of the Thesis

Chapter 2 presents the theoretical background on financial time series, forecasting models, interpretability and explanation evaluation. Chapter 3 reviews the existing literature and identifies the research gap. Chapter 4 explains the experimental design, data, targets, walk-forward splits, model configurations, explanation diagnostics, and reproducibility procedures. Chapter 5 reports the predictive, stability, and faithfulness results. Chapter 6 discusses these results in relation to the three research questions and their practical implications. Chapter 7 presents the main methodological, data, explanation, and external-validity limitations. Chapter 8 concludes with direct answers to the research questions and priorities for future work. The appendices provide detailed result tables, configuration guidance, correction records, provenance, and notation.

This chapter presents the concepts and formal definitions used in the experimental evaluation. Section 2.1 characterizes financial time series as a data-generating environment, their stylized facts, the resulting limits to predictability, and the non-stationarity that motivates the temporal stability question of RQ2. Section 2.2 introduces the forecasting models benchmarked in this thesis, from classical baselines to deep sequence models, and clarifies the role of overfitting. Section 2.3 formalizes interpretability and the post-hoc explanation toolbox, including Shapley-value-based attribution and local surrogate models alongside the broader family of model-agnostic methods.

Section 2.4 reviews how the quality of explanations themselves can be evaluated, covering faithfulness, stability, and the pitfalls that arise when explanations are computed on dependent, non-stationary financial data. Throughout, terms introduced here (post-hoc explanation methods, intrinsically interpretable models, black-box architectures, feature attribution, faithfulness, stability) are used consistently in the remainder of the thesis. Financial Time Series: Properties and Stylized Facts

Empirical research has identified several recurring properties of asset returns, often called stylized facts. Forecasting models and their explanations must be interpreted in light of these properties (Tsay, 2005, pp. 19–20; Green, 2026, para. 18.3.1). This section reviews the four clusters of properties most consequential for this thesis: the non-stationarity of price levels and its resolution through returns, the time-varying volatility of returns, the low signal-to-noise ratio that limits predictability and the prevalence of structural breaks and regime shifts.
Stationarity, Unit Roots, and Log Returns

Stationarity is a foundation of classical time series analysis. A time series rt is strictly stationary if the joint distribution of any finite collection rt1,…,rtk is identical to that of its time-shifted counterpart rt1+τ,…,rtk+τ for all shifts τ. Because this condition is difficult to verify empirically, the weaker notion of weak (or covariance) stationarity is typically assumed, requiring only that the mean and the autocovariances are time-invariant (Tsay, 2005, p. 25; Brockwell & Davis, 2016, Definition 1.4.2). Formally, rt is weakly stationary if
Ert=μ,  Covrt,rt-l=γl

where μ is a constant mean and the autocovariance γl depends only on the lag l, not on time t (Brockwell & Davis, 2016, Definition 1.4.2; Kirchgässner et al., 2013, pp. 12–14). Weak stationarity matters for forecasting because it supports inference from past observations to future ones: as Tsay (2005, p. 25) notes, weak stationarity enables one to make inferences concerning future observations (e.g., prediction).

Most real time series, however, are non-stationary (Aggarwal, 2015, p. 465), and asset prices are a canonical example: for a price series, non-stationarity arises mainly due to the fact that there is no fixed level for the price (Tsay, 2005, p. 64). A series whose stochastic trend does not revert to any fixed level is called unit-root non-stationary, the best-known example being the random walk,
Pt=Pt-1+εt

where Pt is the price at time t and εt is an unpredictable shock. Under such a model the stock price is not predictable or mean-reverting (Tsay, 2005, p. 64) and shocks have permanent effects because their impact does not decay over time (Tsay, 2005, pp. 66–67). A random walk is a special case of non-stationarity in which the characteristic equation of the underlying autoregressive representation has a unit root (Dixon et al., 2020, Ch.6, pp. 195–201).

A standard solution is to model transformed series rather than raw prices. Following the conventions of financial econometrics, this thesis works with (continuously compounded) log returns, defined as the first difference of log prices,
rt=lnPt-lnPt-1

where Pt denotes the closing price at time t. Log returns are approximately stationary, are additive over time, and for daily data differ negligibly from simple net returns (Tsay, 2005, p. 19). The transformation is standard in applied work and is routinely justified by unit-root tests such as the Augmented Dickey–Fuller test, which recent benchmarking practice also uses to characterize the non-stationarity of financial forecasting datasets (Stankiewicz, 2015, p. 15; Hu et al., 2026).

Integrated models of the ARIMA class formalize this idea: an ARIMA p,d,q process is one that reduces to a stationary ARMA process after differencing d times, making such models useful for representing data with trend (Brockwell & Davis, 2016, p. 158).

Empirically, daily returns of market indices and individual stocks exhibit high excess kurtosis, fat tails relative to the normal distribution, while the mean of a daily return series is close to zero, and market indices display smaller standard deviations than individual stocks (Kirchgässner et al., 2013, pp. 18–19; Tsay, 2005, pp. 19–20). These distributional properties matter for this thesis in two ways: they constrain the magnitude of the predictable component in returns (Section 2.1.3), and they imply that explanations attributing predictions to features must be interpreted in an environment where extreme observations are systematic rather than aberrant.
Volatility Clustering, Heteroscedasticity, and the Leverage Effect

While returns themselves are close to serially uncorrelated, they are far from independent, their dependence is concentrated in the second moments. (Tsay, 2005, pp. 98–99) summarizes four characteristics of asset volatility: first, volatility clusters, so that high-volatility periods alternate with calm periods, second, volatility evolves continuously in that jumps are rare, third, volatility does not diverge and is often stationary itself and fourth volatility reacts asymmetrically to large price increases versus large price drops the leverage effect.

Volatility clustering has long been documented: Mandelbrot already observed that small (large) shocks tend to be followed by small (large) shocks, generating leptokurtic return distributions (Kirchgässner et al., 2013, p. 281; Tsay, 2005, pp. 105–108). In an empirical illustration with daily DAX returns, Kirchgässner et al. (2013, pp. 281–283) find a kurtosis far above the Gaussian value of three and strongly autocorrelated squared residuals, which contradicts the assumption of a constant, time-invariant variance.

Conditional heteroscedasticity of this kind is the subject of the ARCH/GARCH family of models, which treat the conditional variance as time-dependent (Dixon et al., 2020, pp. 199–201; Tsay, 2005, Chapter 3). In the notation of this thesis, with rt decomposed as rt=μt+at into a conditional mean μt and an innovation at=σtεt, an ARCH-type model specifies the conditional variance σt2 as a function of past squared innovations, EGARCH-type variants additionally capture the asymmetry induced by large positive and negative returns (Tsay, 2005, pp. 98–99, 124). In line with the delimitation of this thesis, GARCH models enter only as background on the data-generating environment; they are not among the benchmarked models, since the forecasting targets are prices and returns rather than volatility.

Heteroscedasticity is directly relevant to the research questions of this thesis. Regimes of elevated volatility (crisis periods) and calm regimes (bull-market drift) imply that the conditional distribution of returns changes over time even when no structural break in the mean equation occurs. Feature attributions computed globally over a sample that pools such regimes may therefore mask regime-specific model behaviour, a concern formalized in Section 2.4.2 and addressed empirically under RQ2.
Low Signal-to-Noise, Random Walks, and Predictability Limits

Financial theory gives several reasons to expect weak return predictability. If investors were risk neutral, returns would be unpredictable and prices would follow martingales, more generally, prices scaled by marginal utility are martingales, and returns can be predictable only to the extent that investors are risk averse and conditional second moments of returns and discount factors vary over time. A more plausible configuration at long horizons than at short ones (Cochrane, 2005, pp. 21–22). Intuitively, if today’s price lay far below the expected price tomorrow, investors would buy until the discrepancy vanished, so returns should not be predictable and as per Cochrane (2005, pp. 21–22)returns should be like coin flips.

Empirically, returns of indices in efficient markets behave approximately like a pure random process: standard autocorrelation tests such as Ljung–Box and Breusch–Godfrey typically fail to indicate serial correlation, even though normality is clearly rejected because of excess kurtosis (Kirchgässner et al., 2013, pp. 19–20, Example 1.3). Asset returns accordingly exhibit little to no autocorrelation, and past returns contain little information about future returns (Green, 2026, para. 18.3.1).

Together, these properties imply a very low signal-to-noise ratio. Prediction tasks on financial time series are notoriously difficult, since noise dominates the series and markets are generally accepted to be efficient in the semi-strong form (Fischer & Krauss, 2018, p. 654, see Section 1.1.1; López De Prado, 2020a, p. 10, 106) emphasizes that only a small fraction of the information in financial data is signal, which is systematically suppressed by arbitrage forces, and that in a field like financial economics, where the signal-to-noise ratio is low, false strategies abound. Textbook evidence reinforces the point: for daily S&P 500 data, correlations between lagged returns and today’s return are close to zero, and a classifier trained on data up to 2004 achieved a test error rate of 52% in 2005 worse than random guessing (James et al., 2013, pp. 158, 162).

Tsay’s (2005, pp. 180–183) controlled comparison of feed-forward neural networks against a random walk with drift for monthly IBM log returns is the canonical cautionary result: the network’s out-of-sample mean squared forecast error was essentially identical to that of a simple AR(1) and the random-walk benchmark, direction-prediction accuracy varied substantially across estimation runs, and across 500 simulation runs the network does not outperform the simple model that assumes a random walk with drift (Tsay, 2005, p. 183).

These limits shape the design and interpretation of the thesis. First, when predictive accuracy differentials between models are small by construction of the problem, the accuracy – interpretability trade-off examined under RQ1 must be evaluated statistically rather than by point estimates alone. Second, where predictability exists, it is more plausibly attributed to time-varying risk premia than to fixed statistical patterns (Cochrane, 2005, pp. 21–22), so explanations that suggest stable, universal drivers of returns warrant scepticism (RQ3).
Structural Breaks and Regime Shifts

Beyond smooth variation in volatility, financial time series are subject to discrete structural change. A fundamental difficulty is that a time series represents only one realization of a stochastic process, so only special forms of non-stationarity can be handled among them deterministic trends and stochastic (unit-root) trends, with deterministic trends generally inappropriate for long-run forecasts (Kirchgässner et al., 2013, pp. 155–157). Structural breaks can distort unit-root tests. If a series is stationary, or stationary around a trend, a structural break can cause standard tests to indicate a unit root even when none exists. This problem can persist in large samples. Tests that explicitly account for structural breaks, following Perron’s approach, help address this issue (Kirchgässner et al., 2013, pp. 178–179).

In the nonlinear econometric literature, discrete regimes are modelled explicitly, for example through self-exciting threshold autoregressive (SETAR) models in which the dynamics switch between regimes according to the level of the series itself (Tsay, 2005, pp. 161–173).

The machine learning literature describes a related phenomenon as concept drift: the data-generating process changes over time, so recent observations are typically more informative than older ones, which become stale for analytical purposes (Aggarwal, 2015, p. 393) and abrupt drift can be viewed as a change point rather than ordinary noise (Aggarwal, 2015, para. 12.5). For forecasting practice, regime shifts are destructive in a specific way documented by Dixon et al. (2020, pp. 39–40) in the context of mortgage models across the financial crisis: when the evaluation distribution lies in the future, we cannot draw testing data from the distribution we care about, so standard cross-validation cannot rescue a model whose training distribution no longer applies.

The market regimes considered in this thesis include high- and low-volatility periods, bull and bear markets, and crisis episodes. These regimes are not merely descriptive categories. They can violate the stationarity assumptions under which forecasting models and their explanations are estimated. This motivates the temporal-splits discipline and the regime-conditioned evaluation of explanation stability that RQ2 addresses.
Forecasting Models for Financial Time Series

The research design fixes the model set: baselines (linear regression, ARIMA), tree ensembles (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM), and deep sequence models (LSTM, Temporal Fusion Transformer). This section introduces each class at the level required for the experiments, emphasizing the properties that matter for interpretability analysis. One methodological point is important at the outset. Supervised machine learning treats the data-generating process as unknown and replaces classical in-sample diagnostics with out-of-sample evaluation and explicit management of the bias–variance trade-off (Dixon et al., 2020, pp. 16–17). Flexible models can overfit, regardless of their interpretability. Overfitting occurs when a model learns random noise in the training data instead of the underlying pattern. Under squared-error loss, the expected test error consists of squared bias, variance, and irreducible error. More flexible models tend to reduce bias but increase variance (James et al., 2013, pp. 34–37; Kubat, 2015, pp. 81–83; Green, 2026, pp. 74–76).

This risk is separate from interpretability: structurally simple models such as decision trees are themselves prone to overfitting and instability (Chan et al., 2022, pp. 70–76; James et al., 2013, p. 320). The central problem with black-box architectures is therefore not necessarily a greater tendency to overfit. Instead, their overfitting and other failure modes are difficult to diagnose from the model structure. Post-hoc explanation methods are intended to reduce this opacity (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, pp. 8–10, see Section 1.1.4).

Overfitting on the training set can be mitigated by resampling, regularization, and ensembling, whereas overfitting to the test set arises through repeated model selection on the same evaluation data and requires multiple-testing discipline (López De Prado, 2020a, pp. 7–9), the executed protocol and its remaining leakage and comparability limitations are specified in Chapter 4.
Baselines: Linear Regression and ARIMA
Linear regression models the target as an affine function of the input features,
rt=β0+j=1pβjxtj

where xtj is the value of feature j at time t and the coefficients βj are estimated by least squares (James et al., 2013, Chapter 3). Linear regression is the prototypical intrinsically interpretable model: each coefficient can be related directly to the contribution of a feature, which is why structurally restricted models of this kind serve as the interpretable reference point in the trade-off analysis (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, pp. 8–10; Molnar, 2022, pp. 3, 10). Its limitations in the financial context are equally well documented: the assumption of normally distributed, homoscedastic errors is routinely violated by heavy-tailed, skewed financial data (Kim et al., 2026, pp. 49–50) and linearity precludes the interaction effects to which the predictive gains of more flexible methods are commonly attributed (Gu et al., 2020, p. 2223).
ARIMA p,d,q models are the classical time series baseline. An autoregressive component of order p expresses the current value as a linear combination of its own lags,
rt=ϕ0+i=1pϕirt-i+at

where at is a white-noise innovation, the moving-average and integration components extend this recursion, and d orders of differencing accommodate non-stationary series, since ARIMA processes reduce to ARMA processes when differenced finitely many times (Aggarwal, 2015, Chapter 14; Brockwell & Davis, 2016, p. 158). An ARp model is stationary only if the roots of its characteristic equation lie outside the unit circle, a unit root yields the random-walk-type non-stationarity discussed in Section 2.1.1 (Dixon et al., 2020, pp. 195–199; Tsay, 2005, p. 64). ARIMA remains a competitive baseline: large-scale forecasting comparisons have found statistical models to match or exceed the accuracy of machine learning models, including LSTMs, on standard benchmarks (Molnar, 2022, p. 58) and the evidence on LSTM versus ARIMA in financial applications is mixed and context-dependent (Mao et al., 2026, pp. 2–3).
Tree Ensembles: Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM

Single decision trees are highly interpretable, they are even easier to explain than linear regression (James et al., 2013, p. 320) but they are unstable, sensitive to small perturbations of the training data, and prone to overfitting (Chan et al., 2022, pp. 70–76; Kubat, 2015, Chapter 6). Ensemble methods sacrifice this transparency for accuracy. Bagging averages many trees fitted to bootstrap resamples, exploiting the variance reduction of averaging (James et al., 2013, p. 321), Random Forest additionally decorrelates the trees by considering only a random subset of candidate predictors at each split, typically of size p (James et al., 2013, p. 324).

Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially, with each new tree learning from the errors left by earlier trees (James et al., 2013, Chapter 8). XGBoost and LightGBM are regularized, computationally efficient implementations of this approach and are widely used for tabular data. XGBoost, in particular, is commonly applied to financial time-series forecasting (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:20).

The accuracy gain has an interpretability price: once many trees are aggregated, it is no longer possible to represent the resulting statistical learning procedure using a single tree, so bagging improves prediction accuracy at the expense of interpretability (James et al., 2013, p. 323). Ensembles nonetheless retain a weak form of intrinsic interpretability through variable-importance summaries, the average reduction in residual sum of squares or node impurity attributable to each predictor across the trees (James et al., 2013, pp. 323–324, 335). Two cautions attach to such measures and are developed in Section 2.4.3: impurity-based importance is an in-sample quantity, A variable that is statistically significant for explaining patterns within the sample may not be useful for forecasting new observations (López De Prado, 2020a, p. 80) and (Chan et al., 2022, p. 76) also caution that variable-importance measures lack a theoretical basis and should therefore be interpreted carefully.
Deep Learning: Long Short-Term Memory Networks

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) maintain a hidden state that is propagated across time steps, allowing information to persist, in a time series forecasting application, outputs may be required at each time stamp to predict the next value of the series (Aggarwal, 2018, Chapter 7). Plain RNNs suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients over long horizons, which gated architectures address. The Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network augments the recurrent cell with input, forget, and output gates that regulate the flow of information into, within, and out of a cell state, giving the network fine-grained control over what is remembered (Aggarwal, 2018, para. 7.5, pp. 292–297; Green, 2026, para. 7.2.5).

The gated recurrent unit (GRU) is a lighter variant with a smaller parameter footprint (Aggarwal, 2018, pp. 296–297) and in applied work the LSTM has become a standard recurrent baseline (Hull, 2021, p. 265).

For financial markets, the LSTM is the canonical black-box architecture in this thesis. Its parameters, gate weights, cell states, recurrent connections, admit no direct mapping to feature effects, and the architecture is described as uninterpretable in the literature (Aggarwal, 2018, p. 437). Its forecasting credentials in equity markets rest prominently on Fischer and Krauss (2018, p. 654), who report that LSTM networks outperformed random forests, deep feed-forward networks, and logistic regression in directional prediction of S&P 500 constituents over 1992–2015 while also documenting that the LSTM’s excess returns decayed after approximately 2010, fluctuating around zero after transaction costs.
This decay is itself an illustration of regime dependence (RQ2): edges in financial data are arbitraged away as markets adapt.
Attention Mechanisms and Temporal Fusion Transformers

Attention mechanisms equip sequence models with content-dependent weighting of input elements: at each step, the model computes compatibility scores between a query and the keys of candidate inputs and forms a weighted combination of the associated values, so the model makes hard decisions about specific parts of the data to attend to (Aggarwal, 2018, para. 10.2, p.421). Self-attention generalizes this idea by letting queries, keys, and values all derive from the same sequence, combined with positional encoding and stacked encoder–decoder blocks, it defines the transformer architecture (Green, 2026, para. 7.3.10). Because attention weights are recalculated at each time step, the model can in principle adapt to changing temporal relationships, and features deemed irrelevant receive low attention weights that reduce their influence on the output (Habiba et al., 2026, para. 3.5.3, pp. 81–82).

The Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) is the attention-based architecture considered in this thesis. It is representative of a design philosophy that builds interpretability directly into the architecture: variable-selection networks and attention weights are intended to expose which inputs and which time steps drive a prediction, in contrast to purely post-hoc analysis of an opaque model (Habiba et al., 2026, pp. 8–9).

This interpretable-by-design positioning makes the TFT the natural counterpart to the LSTM in the accuracy – interpretability comparison of RQ1. However, whether attention weights constitute reliable explanations is contested, Section 2.3.4 reviews the reliability critique, and the thesis treats attention weights as intrinsic, model-internal attributions whose faithfulness and stability must be evaluated rather than assumed (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:18).

Predictive performance across all models is quantified with root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), directional accuracy, and R², their executed definitions and the limits of the available statistical comparisons are specified in Chapter 4.
Interpretability and Explainable AI

If the models of Section 2.2 differ in how transparently their mechanics can be inspected, the purpose of explainable AI (XAI) is to make the behaviour of the opaque members of that set comprehensible and checkable. This section first disentangles the terminology (Section 2.3.1), then formalizes the intrinsic-versus-post-hoc distinction and the associated trade-off (Section 2.3.2), provides a broad overview of post-hoc explanation methods, with Shapley-value-based and surrogate-based approaches selected for empirical evaluation in this thesis (Section 2.3.3) and closes with the contested status of attention weights as explanations (Section 2.3.4).
Taxonomy: Interpretability, Explainability and Transparency

The vocabulary of the field is unsettled, and terminological confusion is well documented, the terms interpretable and explainable are frequently used interchangeably even in technical publications (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:2). A regulatory analysis of EU legislation likewise concludes that transparency, traceability, interpretability, and explainability remain ill-defined and inconsistently applied, and proposes to treat them as layered, interdependent dimensions of algorithmic opacity, which itself arises at multiple levels from institutional secrecy to the structural inaccessibility of high-dimensional machine learning systems (Buttaboni & Floridi, 2026, para. 1).

This thesis adopts the following working conventions. Interpretability is understood as a graded property of a model relative to a human observer: the degree to which a human can understand the cause of a decision, or, in an operational variant, the degree to which a human can consistently predict the model’s output (Molnar, 2022, p. 8). There is no conclusive mathematical definition of when a model is interpretable, measurable aspects of interpretability can nonetheless be distinguished into human-based evaluations and function-level, mathematical evaluations (Molnar, 2022, p. 9). A model is a black-box when its structure is too complex for humans to understand, for most people the threshold lies closer to ten than to a hundred free parameters and a glass-box (or white-box) when it is easy to understand.

The practical consequence of opacity is that one cannot determine which features influenced a prediction and by how much, making it difficult to decide whether the model is consistent with our domain knowledge (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, pp. 8–10). Following the survey usage in the financial forecasting domain, an interpretable (transparent) model can be understood by direct inspection, whereas an explainable model is a black-box model paired with a distinct explainability method (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:3–265:4). Explanations themselves are distinguished by scope into instance-level (local) and dataset-level (global) accounts (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, p. 7). The field as a whole covers three strands: inherently interpretable models, modifications of complex models towards interpretability, and post-hoc interpretation methods (Molnar, 2022, p. 3).

An ideal predictive model should meet the following three requirements: for every prediction, one should be able to verify the strength of the supporting evidence (prediction’s validation), to understand which variables affect the prediction and to what extent (prediction’s justification), and to anticipate how the prediction would change if the inputs changed (prediction’s speculation) (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, pp. 6–7). These requirements anticipate the evaluation criteria of Section 2.4.
Intrinsic versus Post-hoc Interpretability and the Accuracy – Interpretability Trade-off

RQ1 is motivated by the idea that increasing model flexibility can reduce interpretability: In general, as the flexibility of a method increases, its interpretability decreases (James et al., 2013, p. 25), with subset selection and linear models at the interpretable end and bagging, boosting, and support vector machines at the flexible end. Structurally restricted models such as decision rules or linear models permit component-wise interpretation, whereas well-tuned neural networks and gradient-boosted trees lack any direct mapping from parameters to feature effects (Molnar, 2022, p. 3). Two routes to satisfying explanation requirements follow: use models that are interpretable by design accepting that the price of transparency may be a reduction in performance or keep a complex model and explain its predictions with post-hoc tools that approximate or simplify its behaviour (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, p. 7).

In finance, this trade-off affects practical model choices. Practitioners report considering interpretability when choosing between neural networks and statistical methods, even when the statistical methods are less accurate (Dixon et al., 2020, p. 167). Reviews of XAI in financial decision-making also note that interpretable models, such as decision trees and linear regression, often have lower predictive power than more complex models, such as deep neural networks (Hoang et al., 2026, pp. 206–208).

Three qualifications prevent a naive reading of the trade-off, all of which shape the design of this thesis. First, the trade-off is an empirical regularity, not a law: it is commonly believed that complex ML models always outperform more interpretable models in terms of accuracy. However, there are several examples where interpretable models have proven to be serious competitors, including time series forecasting, where statistical models have systematically outperformed LSTMs and multi-layer perceptrons (Molnar, 2022, pp. 57–58). Second, the trade-off may be reversed by overfitting: even where interpretability is not a concern, the textbook example being stock-price prediction. We will often obtain more accurate predictions using a less flexible method, because highly flexible methods are prone to overfitting (James et al., 2013, p. 26). Third, the Rudin critique, acknowledged across the literature surveyed here, holds that for high-stakes decisions interpretable models should be favoured over explained black boxes, that interpretable models should always be included in benchmarks, and that choosing a black-box model must be justified by a relevant performance increase (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:29–30; Molnar, 2022, p. 3).

Accordingly, the thesis deliberately includes linear and tree-based baselines and investigates how large the trade-off is, rather than whether it exists. A final issue is where to draw the line between intrinsic interpretability and post-hoc explanation. A model is usually considered intrinsically interpretable when people can relate its individual components to real-world concepts. In complex models, however, interpreting these components can make this distinction unclear (Molnar, 2022, p. 13). The debate over whether attention weights provide meaningful explanations is one example of this problem (Section 2.3.4).
Post-hoc Explanation Methods

Post-hoc explanation methods analyse an already trained model without altering it. Model-agnostic variants require access only to the prediction function, not to internal parameters, so the same method can be applied to a neural network, a random forest, or a linear model, this modularity also enables comparison of explanations across models (Molnar, 2022, p. 11). Mechanistically, most such methods follow a common pipeline sampling data, applying an intervention to features, obtaining predictions, and aggregating the results formalized as the SIPA framework (Molnar, 2022, p. 14).
