Attention Weights as Explanations and Their Reliability

Because attention weights are produced inside the model during the forward pass, they are often presented as intrinsic explanations: they are intuitive, model-internal, and in architectures such as the TFT they form part of the advertised interpretability (Habiba et al., 2026, pp. 8–9, 90). Classifying attention as ante-hoc or post-hoc is itself nuanced: the weights are computed within the model (suggesting ante-hoc status), yet the attention distribution may be an unintended by-product of optimization rather than a designed explanation, arguing for a post-hoc reading (Spinnato, 2023, p. 23). In the taxonomy of XAI for time series, attentions are built into the model as an ante-hoc mechanism, whereas attribution methods operate post-hoc on fixed trained models (Theissler et al., 2022).

However, substantial criticisms concern the reliability of attention weights. Empirical comparisons reviewed in the financial forecasting literature find that attention weights contain some useful information about the feature importance, but the information may not be enough to correctly rank the features, that attention-based rankings show low correlation with gradient-based and leave-one-out rankings, and that if a reliable interpretation has to be plausible and faithful, then attention weights would not be reliable (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:18). Reported results diverge across contexts, definitions, and testing methods, so the reliability of the interpretation of complex models must be challenged, and their use must be done with caution (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 18), comparatively, attention weights are not always faithful and vary by attention head (Habiba et al., 2026, p. 90).

These criticisms do not make attention weights useless, but they must be evaluated empirically. In this thesis, TFT attention weights are treated as one internal signal of model behavior and are examined alongside post-hoc attributions in the stability and faithfulness analyses (RQ2 and RQ3). They are not assumed to be faithful explanations simply because the model produces them.
Evaluating Explanations

An explanation is not trustworthy simply because a method can produce one. Explanations must be evaluated along criteria that the literature converges on comprehensibility, fidelity, accuracy, stability, and completeness even though these theoretical concepts are difficult to quantify (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:24). This thesis operationalizes three of them: faithfulness (this section, 2.4.1), stability (2.4.2), and robustness to the known pitfalls of explanation methods on financial data (2.4.3).

Evaluation is difficult because there is no ground truth against which an explanation can be compared, which complicates the study of interpretability itself (Molnar, 2022, p. 9) and because gold-standard time series datasets with annotated discriminative regions do not yet exist (Theissler et al., 2022).
Faithfulness

Faithfulness describes how accurate an explanation fits a model’s behavior towards the prediction score, the same construct circulates under the names perturbation analysis, ablation study, trustworthiness, or fidelity (Theissler et al., 2022, p. 100715). For surrogate-based explanations, fidelity has a direct quantitative reading: the degree to which the interpretable model reproduces the black-box’s outputs measured as agreement of predicted labels in classification and, for regression, as the mean squared or mean absolute error between surrogate and black-box predictions, a quantity that is admittedly rarely assessed in regression settings (Spinnato, 2023, pp. 38–39). The standard experimental protocol is perturbation-based: an explanation is computed, the features or time points identified as most relevant are altered to non-informative values, and the resulting degradation of the prediction is observed, a large degradation indicates that the explanation identified genuinely load-bearing inputs (Theissler et al., 2022, p. 100715).

Deletion-and insertion-type procedures instantiate this protocol by progressively removing (respectively re-adding) features in order of attributed importance and tracking the prediction curve, with area-based summaries such as AOPCR and ablation thresholds such as APT proposed as quantitative faithfulness measures for time series prediction (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:25).

Two caveats are especially important for financial time series. First, perturbation requires a non-information holding baseline value, and in time series such values are not easy to identify zero, for instance, may itself carry meaning and alter the semantics of an observation so perturbation strategies must be chosen deliberately and reported as part of the evaluation design (Spinnato, 2023, p. 39; Theissler et al., 2022, p. 100715). Second, the protocol inherits the tunable parameters of the perturbation scheme, which might lead to different results when being used by different researchers (Theissler et al., 2022).

A further structural caveat distinguishes explanation quality from model quality: an interpretation can only be as good as its underlying model, since an overfit or underfit model distorts apparent feature effects, and different methods answer different questions Shapley-based measures expose the features a model mechanistically uses, whereas test-set permutation importance reflects what contributes to generalization (Molnar, 2022, pp. 5–6 of the pitfalls chapter).
Stability of Explanations

Stability denotes the consistency of an explanation when applied to similar instances (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:24). The temporal dimension is central to this thesis: explanations computed from models retrained on different windows, or queried in different market regimes, should agree if they reflect durable structure rather than sample-specific noise. Empirical studies support this concern. Explanation methods applied to time series models may suffer from instability, lack of consistency, and temporal misalignment, with SHAP and LIME characterized as computationally expensive, unstable over time (Habiba et al., 2026, pp. 89–90). In applied economic modelling, overall variable importance has been found fairly stable across country groups, while the magnitudes of feature impacts still differ over time (Fourné, 2026, p. 44) a pattern consistent with stable rankings but unstable attributions.

Even for a fixed dataset and model class, different explainers can produce highly variant explanations for the same underlying ML model, suggesting different parts of the input data to be the potential cause for a given prediction (Theissler, 2024, para. 3.2). And the training process itself is an ignored source of uncertainty, since standard methods quantify only the Monte Carlo approximation error of the explanation given a fixed model (Molnar, 2022, pp. 29–30). Architectural choices compound the problem: for rectified networks, increasing the number of hidden units provably increases a bound on the variance of the model’s Jacobian, and hence reduces the stability of sensitivity-based interpretations (Dixon et al., 2020, pp. 173–174).

In non-stationary environments, feature relevance itself drifts features relevant today (e.g., volatility indicators) may lose significance tomorrow (Habiba et al., 2026, p. 156). Stability therefore determines whether attributions can inform decisions across regimes. It is not merely a desirable presentational property, its quantification under structural breaks and regime shifts is the subject of RQ2.
Known Pitfalls: Dependent Features, Extrapolation, and Multiple Comparisons

The literature identifies three recurring pitfalls that directly threaten explanation validity in financial time series. The first concerns feature dependence. Perturbation-based methods PDP, PFI, LIME, and Shapley-based attributions alike manipulate features individually, when features are correlated, the intervened data have a different distribution than the training data, and might even lie outside the convex hull of the data and represent physically impossible entities (Molnar, 2022, p. 4). The model is then evaluated in areas of the feature space with few or no observed real data points, where model uncertainty can be expected to be very high, which can produce misleading interpretations (Molnar, 2022, p. 9 of the pitfalls chapter). Financial feature sets lagged returns, rolling volatility estimates, overlapping technical indicators are strongly dependent by construction, and financial datasets are highly multicollinear because of shared risk factors (López De Prado, 2020a, pp. 76–77).

Conditional variants that resample from conditional rather than marginal distributions mitigate extrapolation but change the estimand itself: in the extreme case of duplicated features, conditional importance approaches zero for both, and it would be a pitfall to conclude that both are irrelevant (Molnar, 2022, pp. 24–25). The financial literature documents the same phenomenon as substitution effects: when two features share predictive information, impurity-based importance is split between them, and permutation-based importance may judge both unimportant even if they are critical, clustering or orthogonalization of features is the proposed, imperfect remedy (López De Prado, 2020a, pp. 81, 84–85).

The second pitfall is extrapolation beyond the training distribution. This problem is related to feature dependence but is conceptually distinct: even marginally valid perturbations can place the model in regions where its behaviour is unconstrained by data, so the explanation reports properties of an untested function rather than of the fitted relationship (Molnar, 2022, p. 23). The third pitfall is multiple comparisons. Simultaneously testing the importance of many features at a fixed significance level virtually guarantees false positives with 50 features tested at α=0.05, the probability of at least one spuriously significant feature is approximately 0.92 under the global null and remedies such as Bonferroni-type corrections, knockoff procedures, or resampling-based significance calibration exist but are rarely applied (Molnar, 2022, pp. 20–21 of the pitfalls chapter).

The same logic is familiar from data mining practice, where querying the data from enough angles makes a chance finding near-certain (Bruce et al., 2020, pp. 112–115) and from financial backtesting, where repeated trials on the same series inflate apparent performance selection bias under multiple testing (López De Prado, 2020a, pp. 105–107). Explanation evaluation comparing attributions across many features, models, markets, and regimes is exposed to exactly this risk, which the experimental protocol of Chapter 4 addresses.

Sections 2.3 and 2.4 therefore establish two premises for the empirical analysis: post-hoc explanation methods offer a principled, model-agnostic toolbox for opening black-box forecasting models, but their outputs are approximations whose faithfulness, stability, and robustness to dependent financial features cannot be assumed. The literature review in Chapter 3 situates these foundations within empirical evidence on explainable machine learning for financial forecasting and derives the three research gaps that the experiments of Chapters 4 and 5 address.

This chapter reviews and synthesizes the literature at the intersection of financial time series forecasting, interpretable machine learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Consistent with the delimitation of this thesis, the review covers supervised machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches to daily-to-monthly stock price and return forecasting, and treats autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) and generalized autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity (GARCH) models as classical benchmarks rather than as objects of explanation. The chapter proceeds thematically rather than chronologically. Section 3.1 traces the move from linear benchmarks to ML/DL predictors and the evaluation-rigor literature that accompanies it.

Section 3.2 examines interpretability in financial ML, including the contested accuracy – interpretability trade-off and the economic meaning of feature importance. Section 3.3 reviews XAI methods as applied in finance and in time series analysis more broadly, together with emerging benchmarking standards. Section 3.4 synthesizes evidence on the stability, faithfulness, and economic plausibility of explanations. Section 3.5 consolidates the review into three research gaps and maps them to the research questions of this thesis.
Machine Learning for Financial Market Prediction
From Linear Benchmarks to Machine Learning and Deep Learning

The point of departure for any forecasting study on equity data is the near-unpredictability implied by asset-pricing theory. Under risk neutrality, prices follow martingales and returns are unpredictable, more generally, predictability is possible only if investors are risk averse and conditional moments of returns and discount factors vary over time (Cochrane, 2005, pp. 21–22). Empirically, daily returns of market indices and individual stocks exhibit high excess kurtosis and a mean close to zero, so the exploitable signal is small relative to noise (Tsay, 2005, p. 9) and financial series are relatively short, serially correlated, multicollinear and possibly nonstationary (López De Prado, 2020a, p. 105).

Consequently, the random walk is the canonical benchmark in forecasting exercises (Hull, 2021, p. 109) and prediction tasks on financial time series are notoriously difficult, owing to their high noise content and generally accepted semi-strong market efficiency (Fischer & Krauss, 2018, p. 654, see Section 1.1.1). Against this baseline, classical linear models such as ARIMA and GARCH remain the reference points that any ML or DL predictor must beat out of sample (Medeiros, 2022; Tsay, 2005).

Large-scale comparative studies report that flexible ML and DL models can indeed outperform linear benchmarks. In a cross-sectional horse race over roughly 30,000 U.S. stocks and 94 characteristics, (Gu et al., 2020) find that trees and neural networks achieve the best out-of-sample performance, trace their gains to nonlinear predictor interactions missed by other methods and report that ML-based long–short portfolios attain an annualized out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 0.77 against 0.51 for leading regression-based strategies (2020, pp. 2223–2226). For time-series directional prediction, Fischer and Krauss (2018, p. 654) show that long short-term memory (LSTM) networks applied to S&P 500 constituents (1992–2015) outperform memory-free classifiers (random forest, a deep neural network, logistic regression), earning daily returns of 0.46 percent and a Sharpe ratio of 5.8 before transaction costs.

These results motivate the inclusion of black-box architectures, gradient-boosted trees and recurrent or transformer networks in the model set of this thesis, and they exemplify the shift, described by Dixon et al. (2020, pp. 16–17) from classical fit statistics toward out-of-sample predictive performance as the governing criterion in financial modeling.

The superiority of flexible models is, however, far from uniform, and the same literature contains instructive negative and mixed results. Tsay’s (2005, pp. 180–183) Examples 4.7 – 4.8 remain a canonical cautionary case: for monthly IBM log returns, a 3-2-1 feed-forward network attains an out-of-sample mean squared forecast error (MSFE) of 91.74, essentially identical to an AR(1) model (91.70) and a random walk with drift (91.85), while an 8-4-1 network fails to outperform the random-walk benchmark in direction prediction, moreover, repeated estimations of the same architecture produce MSFE values ranging from 89.46 to 93.65, revealing substantial estimation instability. Similarly, James et al. (2013, p. 162) report that a logistic model for daily S&P 500 direction, evaluated on a strict temporal holdout, attains a test error rate of 52 percent worse than random guessing.

Reviewing more recent work, Mao et al. (2026, pp. 2–3) document context-dependent findings: LSTMs outperform ARIMA for monthly market indices in some studies, whereas ARIMA is superior for daily cryptocurrency prices in others, and hybrid ARIMA – LSTM constructions attempt to combine both strengths. At the level of forecasting competitions, evidence summarized by Molnar (2022, pp. 57–58) indicates that statistical models can consistently outperform ML approaches, including LSTMs, in time series forecasting tasks. Taken together, these studies suggest that black-box models can outperform simpler models in some large-scale financial forecasting settings, but this advantage is not consistent. It depends on the forecast horizon, the market, and the evaluation design. These factors must be considered when studying the accuracy–interpretability trade-off (Section 3.2) and the stability of explanations (Section 3.4).
Overfitting, Backtest Overfitting, and Evaluation Rigor

A second strand of the literature concerns the conditions under which reported predictive gains can be trusted at all. López de Prado (2020a, pp. 7–9) distinguishes two types of overfitting: training-set overfitting, in which a specification so flexible that it explains not only the signal, but also the noise is chosen, and test-set overfitting, in which repeated evaluation on the same test set induces a selection bias. Two clarifications from this literature are central to the framing of this thesis. First, overfitting risk is independent of interpretability: intrinsically interpretable models such as decision trees and polynomial classifiers overfit noisy training data as readily as neural networks do(James et al., 2013, p. 320; Kubat, 2015, pp. 81–83, 114–115).

The difficulty posed by black-box architectures is thus not excessive overfitting but opaque failure: an interpretation can only be as good as its underlying model (Molnar, 2022, p. 6 of the embedded pitfalls chapter) and a black box offers no direct way to inspect what has been learned. Second, because financial datasets exhibit low signal-to-noise ratios, false discoveries are mechanically abundant in this field (López De Prado, 2020a, p. 106; see Section 2.1.3) and the same flexibility that produces genuine gains in one regime can manufacture illusory gains in a backtest.

The backtest-overfitting literature quantifies this danger. López de Prado (2020b, p. 105) defines selection bias under multiple testing (SBuMT): it is easy to overfit a backtest by conducting multiple historical simulations and reporting the best, so that most published discoveries in finance are likely false, due to test set overfitting (p. 8). His false strategy theorem shows that the expected maximum Sharpe ratio across trials is strictly positive even when every strategy has a true Sharpe ratio of zero (pp. 108–109), motivating multiplicity-adjusted criteria such as the deflated Sharpe ratio and combinatorial purged cross-validation (pp. 113–124). The same logic appears in the general statistical literature as alpha inflation: with enough queries of the same data, something will emerge as “significant” just by chance (Bruce et al., 2020, pp. 112–115) and selecting comparisons after inspecting the data constitutes data snooping (Montgomery, 2017, pp. 92–93).

Empirically, Bauer (2025, Chapter 3) reports that models selected by a model confidence set (MCS) procedure can show significantly worse out-of-sample than in-sample performance, i.e., exhibit backtest overfitting even under a disciplined selection protocol. This body of work matters for the present thesis beyond its predictive implications: if reported accuracy differences between intrinsically interpretable models and black-box architectures may partly reflect selection bias, then any evaluation of the accuracy – interpretability trade-off must itself be multiplicity-aware.

In response, a methodological consensus on evaluation rigor has formed. Gu et al. (2020, pp. 2244–2248) employ strict chronological train/validation/test splitting with hyperparameter tuning on the validation period only, comparing models with a modified Diebold–Mariano (DM) test, Medeiros (2022, pp. 111–120) systematizes forecast comparison via the DM test, the Li–Liao–Quaedvlieg test, and the MCS under rolling or expanding estimation windows and Mao et al. (2026) validate their multi-model comparisons with the Bonferroni–Dunn procedure. For time-ordered data, Dixon et al. (2020, pp. 213–214) prescribe walk-forward (sliding-window) cross-validation to avoid look-ahead bias, and Green (2026, p. 82) warns that hyperparameter tuning is itself a form of learning through which information about the validation data can leak into the model.

The parsimony principle articulated in the forecasting literature that simpler models are usually preferable out of sample because complexity enlarges the scope for data mining (Diebold, 2007) supplies the evaluative prior against which flexibility must justify itself. What this literature provides is a mature apparatus for comparing predictive accuracy, what it does not provide is any comparable apparatus for comparing the explanations that models produce. This asymmetry is taken up in Sections 3.3 and 3.4.
Interpretability in Financial Machine Learning
The Accuracy–Interpretability Trade-off in Finance

The claim that predictive accuracy and interpretability stand in tension is a standard tenet of statistical learning, which holds that interpretability decreases as a method’s flexibility increases (James et al., 2013, p. 25,see Section 2.3.2) Notably, the canonical textbook statement uses stock prediction itself as the example in which interpretability is supposedly dispensable yet immediately qualifies that even then we will often obtain more accurate predictions using a less flexible method, owing to overfitting in highly flexible methods (James et al., 2013, p. 26). Biecek and Burzykowski (2021, pp. 6–7) describe three requirements for model explanations: validation, justification, and speculation about predictions. These requirements can be met either through models that are interpretable by design or through post-hoc approximation methods. The authors also note that greater transparency may come at the cost of predictive performance (p. 7).

Molnar (2022, pp. 3, 10) attributes the tension to structural restrictions: interpretable models constrain the hypothesis space, so when the best solution lies outside that space, flexibility and interpretability diverge. Terminologically, this literature distinguishes black-box from glass-box models, while noting that interpretability itself lacks a conclusive mathematical definition (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, pp. 8–10; Molnar, 2022, p. 9).

In finance, the trade-off is not merely technical but institutional. Dixon et al. (2020, p. 167) report that interpretability is a prominent issue for practitioners in deciding whether to use neural networks in favor of other machine learning and statistical methods sometimes even if the latter’s predictive accuracy is inferior, and Hull (2021, p. 135) notes that interpretability can be a legal requirement in credit modeling. Review chapters in recent finance volumes restate the trade-off as a central obstacle: highly interpretable models such as decision trees or linear regression are said to lack the predictive power of more complex models like deep neural networks, with Rudin’s argument invoked that interpretable models should be favored in high-stakes decisions (Hoang et al., 2026, p. 207).

Similar formulations appear in Saratchandran (2025, p. 309) and for a gradient-boosting application with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) in Dorak and Yakar (2025, pp. 111–112). These accounts converge on the diagnosis but are largely narrative: they assert, rather than measure, the performance cost of transparency in financial applications.

A counter-literature questions whether the trade-off is as steep as commonly assumed. Molnar (2022, pp. 57–58) warns against using an opaque, complex ML model when an interpretable model would have been sufficient, citing benchmark evidence in which simple models achieve the bulk of the predictive power of complex ones, statistical models outperform ML in time series forecasting competitions, and ensembles fail to beat logistic regression in clinical and credit-scoring domains, his design recommendation is that complex models should only be favored if the additional performance gain is both significant and relevant. In a small-sample financial application, Supsermpol et al. (2026, p. 99) likewise find that random forests outperform both logistic regression and more complex alternatives because complex algorithms struggle with overfitting on limited data.

In their survey of XAI for financial time series forecasting, Arsenault et al. (2025, p. 265:29–265:30) present both positions: the high-stakes argument for intrinsically interpretable models and the rejoinder that matching black-box accuracy with an interpretable design often takes more time and effort, so that a trade-off may hold in certain cases. The disagreement is partly definitional (what counts as interpretable) and partly empirical (which dataset, horizon, and market). For stock price and return forecasting specifically, the magnitude of the trade-off and whether post-hoc explanation methods can relax it, remains an open, task-dependent empirical question, which this thesis addresses under RQ1.
Feature Importance and Economic Meaning

If models are to be interpreted, the dominant currency of interpretation in financial ML is feature importance, and here the literature offers both a methodological program and a set of pointed warnings. López de Prado (2020a, pp. 75–77) argues that the classical instrument of variable selection, the p-value, suffers from four flaws strong distributional assumptions, fragility under multicollinearity, answering the wrong probability question and in-sample significance that need not imply out-of-sample forecasting value and demonstrates in a controlled experiment that p-values misrank informative, redundant, and noise features in ways that [this] casts a doubt over decades of empirical research in Finance (p. 75).

As substitutes he develops mean decrease impurity (MDI) and mean decrease accuracy (MDA) the latter sometimes also known as permutation importance (p. 81), which evaluate importance in cross-validated out-of-sample experiments rather than in-sample (pp. 77–82). Crucially, he cautions that MDI is an in-sample measure, so that a variable significant for explanatory purposes in-sample may nonetheless be irrelevant for forecasting out of sample (p. 80; see Section 2.2.2) an early statement of the faithfulness problem for importance measures.

A second warning concerns correlated features. Because financial predictors share common risk factors, substitution effects arise when two features share predictive information can bias the results from feature importance methods. MDI halves the importance of duplicate features, while MDA may deem two identical but critical features unimportant (López De Prado, 2020b, p. 84) his preferred remedy is clustered feature importance computed on groups of related predictors (pp. 84–85). Molnar (2022, pp. 23–25) examines the same issue in machine learning. When features are dependent, permutation and perturbation methods can create feature combinations in regions with little or no observed data. Evaluating a model in these unsupported regions creates a trade-off between avoiding extrapolation beyond the data and faithfully representing the model’s behavior.

Since the lagged returns, rolling volatility measures, and technical indicators used in stock forecasting are strongly dependent by construction, these substitution and extrapolation effects are not edge cases but the expected operating condition for any feature-attribution method applied to financial time series.

The deepest caution is epistemological: importance is a measurement, not a mechanism. Gu et al. (2020, pp. 2258–2259) operationalize variable importance through predictive R² losses from nullifying a predictor and through squared partial derivatives explicitly framing the interpretive goal as modest yet they emphasize that these improved predictions are only measurements. The measurements do not tell us about economic mechanisms or equilibria (p. 2229). The econometrics literature concurs that predictive estimators should not be read as structural quantities: direct interpretation of ML estimates stretches the method beyond its intended use, prediction (Chan et al., 2022, para. 3.3.2) and ensemble variable-importance scores do not have any theoretical basis and as such cannot be used with confidence (Chan et al., 2022, pp. 70–76). From the modeling side, Dixon et al. (Dixon et al., 2020, pp. 168, 186) add that black-box effect measures such as partial dependence plots ignore interactions and offer no one-to-one correspondence with regression coefficients, limiting the theoretical insight they afford into how architecture choices shape interpretations.

Finally, López de Prado (2020b, p. 9) reminds readers that a backtest may insinuate that a strategy is profitable, but [does] not tell us why, because historical simulation is not a controlled experiment. Relative to this literature, the present thesis adopts López de Prado’s feature-importance program but extends it in two directions he does not pursue. It evaluates post-hoc attribution methods such as SHAP and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) which he mentions only in passing (2020, p. 77) and it tests their temporal stability and faithfulness rather than their ranking properties alone.
Explainable AI for Financial Time Series
XAI Methods Applied in Finance

The XAI literature distinguishes two routes to interpretability. Arsenault et al. (2025, p. 265:2–265:4) separate interpretable models, designed in such a way that users can intuitively understand [their] inner workings, from explainable models, defined as black-box models enhanced with specific explainability methods, such as Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) or Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), while cautioning that the two terms are often used interchangeably in the literature. Molnar (2022, p. 3) partitions the field into three strands inherently interpretable models, interpretability enhancing modifications of complex models, and post-hoc interpretation methods and characterizes model-agnostic methods as those that probe the prediction function without access to model internals (p. 11).

Following this taxonomy and to avoid narrowing the field prematurely, this thesis treats SHAP and LIME as prominent examples within a broader post-hoc explanation toolbox that also includes permutation feature importance (PFI), partial dependence plots (PDP) and accumulated local effects (ALE), and counterfactual explanations (Molnar, 2022, pp. 15–21), alongside model-internal signals such as global feature importance and attention weights. Shapley-based attributions rest on the axiomatic foundation of efficiency, dummy, symmetry, and additivity, for which Shapley values are the unique solution (Molnar, 2022, p. 28; Nguyen et al., 2026, pp. 7–8).

Applications of these methods in finance are documented in several recent surveys and edited volumes, with SHAP emerging as the de facto standard. Arsenault et al. (2025, p. 265:29) find SHAP to be the most prevalent among explainability methods in financial time series forecasting, a popularity they attribute to its mathematical foundation and ease of use and they note that TreeSHAP is particularly useful given the popularity of extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) in this domain (p. 265:20). Hoang et al. (2026, pp. 198–199, 205–206) describe LIME’s local-surrogate formulation and SHAP’s dual local – global capability, and argue that for stock market prediction such techniques enhance transparency, allowing traders and analysts to validate AI-driven insights, they additionally cover counterfactual explanations as an auditing mechanism (para. 3.3).

Worked finance applications remain predominantly classification–oriented and cross-sectional: Dorak and Yakar (2025, pp. 101, 111–112) apply SHAP to a gradient-boosting model of dividend propensity for European firms and Sivasamy (2025, pp. 220–224) reports a credit-default case study in which gradient boosting (AUC 0.92) improves over a logistic baseline (AUC 0.82) with global feature importances attached. In a derivatives–calibration context, Green (2026, pp. 539–540) summarizes evidence that local methods such as LIME, layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) and DeepLIFT can be less effective for deep networks, and that global game-theoretic methods yield more reliable and consistent insights, while also reporting the caution that local interpretability may not align with financial intuition.

Three limitations of this applied literature are consistent across sources. First, its evidentiary base is thin: the finance–oriented chapters are narrative reviews that assert the benefits of XAI without evaluating explanations empirically (Hoang et al., 2026; Valsala Saratchandran, 2025, pp. 306–309) and even the broad technical survey of Habiba et al. (2026, pp. 8–9) concludes that post-hoc tools such as SHAP remain partial, advocating that interpretability be embedded as a first-class architectural constraint (as in the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) or N-BEATS). Second, post-hoc explanations carry an intrinsic fidelity caveat: because the explanation is a separate artifact not tied to the model itself, its fidelity can be questioned (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:19, see Section 1.2).

Third, the methods were largely developed for independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) tabular data: LIME’s locality is hard to define especially when segmenting and replacing the time series (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:21–265:22) and model-agnostic techniques in general may not be suitable for models in which the model output depends also on [a] sequence of previous inputs (Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, p. 11). Each limitation foreshadows one of the research gaps consolidated in Section 3.5.
XAI for Time Series: Classification-Side Evidence

The most systematic treatment of XAI for temporal data comes from the classification side. Theissler et al. (2022, p. 100700) provide the first extensive review of XAI for time series classification, organizing methods into time–point-based, subsequence–based and instance–based explanations and characterizing them along the dimensions of ante-hoc versus post-hoc, model-agnostic versus model-specific, and local versus global. Two of their findings are directly relevant here. Methodologically, they identify faithfulness analysis as the most prominent and widely used quantitative evaluation, in which the parts of a sample deemed relevant by an explanation are perturbed to non-informative values and the resulting change in prediction quality is observed (Theissler et al., 2022, p. 100715).

However, they emphasize that time series lack an obvious non-informative baseline zero could have a specific meaning altering the class membership so perturbation design itself becomes a methodological choice with multiple proposed alternatives. Substantively, they conclude that there is not one best explanation method to use for all models, but rather a heavy dependence on the applied model’s approach, and that subsequence and instance–based methods for multivariate series remain scarce despite their practical relevance (Theissler et al., 2022).

The same review is pointed about the state of evaluation practice. Quantitative assessment is quite frequently done using author–selected examples, showing that the approach is plausible and where a quantitative criterion is used it is typically predictive accuracy yet accuracy can not assess the methods’ interpretability (Theissler et al., 2022). The authors call for gold-standard datasets with annotations of the truly discriminative temporal regions, noting that such datasets are not available yet, and observe that perturbation–based evaluation has a number of parameters itself, which might lead to different results when being used by different researchers.

Complementary work deepens these concerns: Theissler (2024, para. 3.1) argues that for most time series the pure localization of influential inputs is not a sufficient explanation (the non-inherent semantics problem) and Spinnato (2023, pp. 38–39) notes that fidelity the agreement between a surrogate or explanation and the black-box model is routinely assessed for classification but rarely assessed for regression, where it could nonetheless be computed as the mean squared or absolute error between surrogate and black-box outputs.

For the present thesis, this classification-side evidence plays a dual role. On the one hand, it supplies evaluation protocols perturbation–based faithfulness tests, surrogate–fidelity scores that can be transferred to forecasting and Spinnato’s (Spinnato, 2023, pp. 38–39) regression-fidelity formulation makes that transfer explicit. On the other hand, the transfer must be argued rather than assumed: forecasting is a regression task on continuous, overlapping, non-stationary observations, not a classification task on discrete labeled series and the perturbation–baseline problem identified by Theissler et al. (2022) is arguably aggravated for price and return series, where masked segments, zeroed returns, or interpolated values all encode economic meaning.

Kraft (2025, p. 17) adds a further caution from the clinical domain: approximate SHAP computations may misattribute or miss critical features, and such faithfulness concerns reflect a broader challenge with post-hoc methods rather than a defect of any single algorithm. The classification literature thus demonstrates that quantitative explanation evaluation is feasible while simultaneously showing that the financial forecasting setting remains essentially unserved by it.
Benchmarking and Evaluation Standards: FinTSB and Monash

A precondition for cumulative progress in any empirical field is shared benchmarking infrastructure and two recent contributions define the state of the art for the forecasting side of this thesis. Hu et al. (2026) introduce FinTSB a benchmark for financial time series forecasting motivated by three diagnosed failures of prior evaluation practice: a diversity gap (failure to cover the full spectrum of stock movement patterns) a standardization deficit (absence of unified assessment protocols that would permit cross-study comparison) and a real-world mismatch (neglect of market structure factors such as transaction costs, which inflates reported performance).

FinTSB characterizes its datasets by Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) tests for unit roots to select series with pronounced non-stationarity and low signal-to-noise, enforces temporal ordering to eliminate data leakage and evaluates performance consistency across market regimes (Hu et al., 2026). Complementarily the Monash Time Series Forecasting Archive (Godahewa et al., 2021) provides twenty public datasets spanning domains and frequencies with baseline results reported across eight error metrics and demonstrates the potential of global models trained across collections of series.

These benchmarks converge with the evaluation–rigor literature of Section 3.1.2 on the importance of leakage-aware temporal splitting, multi-metric reporting, and regime-aware assessment evaluation priorities that this thesis examines while disclosing the executed design’s remaining leakage and comparability limitations. Their shared blind spot is equally instructive: neither benchmark contains any provision for evaluating explanations. Predictive quality is standardized, interpretability is not. This observation aligns with the conclusion of Arsenault et al. (2025, p. 265:30) that most XAI models have not been tested with the same benchmarks, leaving the selection among explanation approaches challenging and with the call of Theissler et al. (2022) for rigorous, quantitative and automatic evaluation protocols.

The experimental design of this thesis can therefore be described as layering an explainability–evaluation track stability, faithfulness, and computational overhead metrics onto the financial and general-purpose forecasting benchmarks that the field has recently consolidated.
Stability, Faithfulness, and Economic Plausibility of Explanations
The Explanation Instability and Variance Problem

Research increasingly demonstrates that explanations are not constant but can evolve. Theissler (2024, para. 3.2) articulates the variance problem: well-trained models of comparable performance should reasonably yield comparable explanations, yet experimental studies show that different XAI methods can produce highly divergent explanations of the same underlying ML model, implicating different parts of the input data as the potential cause of a given prediction (reporting results of Bodria et al., as cited in Theissler, 2024, see Section 2.4.2). For time series models specifically, Habiba et al. (2026, p. 90, Table 3.9) catalog the weaknesses of the main explanation families: attention weights are not always faithful and vary by attention head, saliency maps are sensitive to noise and lack temporal scope, and SHAP/LIME are computationally expensive and unstable over time.

The same authors note that in non-stationary series features relevant today (e.g., volatility indicators) may lose significance tomorrow (Habiba et al., 2026, p. 156, Table 5.2) so that explanation instability in finance is not only a property of the explainer but a plausible consequence of the data–generating process itself.

The literature identifies several distinct mechanisms that generate instability and financial time series activate all of them. First, feature dependence: when predictors are correlated, perturbation–based methods extrapolate into unrealistic regions of the feature space, producing misleading or fragile attributions (Molnar, 2022, pp. 23–25) and substitution effects split or suppress importance across related features (López De Prado, 2020b, p. 84). Second, estimation variance: standard explanation practice treats the trained model as fixed and ignores the uncertainty in the training process itself (Molnar, 2022, pp. 29–30), while Dixon et al. (2020, pp. 173–174) prove for a shallow network class that increasing the number of hidden units increases the variance bound of the model’s Jacobian formally linking model capacity to the instability of sensitivity-based interpretations.

Third, regime shifts: structural breaks undermine unit-root inference and more broadly, any global summary of a time-varying relationship (Kirchgässner et al., 2013, pp. 178–179) and cross-validation cannot repair models under distribution shift since that distribution comes from the future (Dixon et al., 2020, pp. 39–40). The temporal decay documented at the model level. Fischer and Krauss (2018, p. 654) find LSTM profitability fluctuating around zero after 2010 as the earlier edge was arbitraged away, implies that any attribution extracted from such a model is indexed to a particular market regime.

Direct evidence on attribution stability over time is nonetheless scarce and incidental. In an applied Shapley analysis of a fiscal-risk index, Fourné (2026, p. 44) reports that overall variable importance is fairly stable across country groups, while the magnitudes of individual variables’ impacts differ over time, in a small-sample corporate–finance application, Supsermpol et al. (2026, p. 99) observe the relative importance of predictors shifting over time as firms mature.

Both remarks are by products of studies with other primary aims and neither quantifies stability formally. To date, no study in the reviewed corpus systematically measures the temporal stability of post-hoc feature attributions for stock price or return forecasting models across regimes such as bull and bear markets or crisis periods. This silence motivates RQ2.
Faithfulness versus Plausibility: The Attention-Is-Not-Explanation Debate

Even where explanations are stable, they may fail to reflect the model they purport to describe. The evaluation literature distinguishes faithfulness how accurately an explanation fits the model’s behavior toward its predictions, a notion appearing under the synonyms perturbation analysis, ablation study, trustworthiness, or fidelity (Theissler et al., 2022, p. 100715) from plausibility, the degree to which an explanation is convincing to humans. Arsenault et al. (2025, p. 265:24) adopt the related criteria of comprehensibility, fidelity, accuracy, stability and completeness, while cautioning that these theoretical concepts are difficult to quantify.

Operationalizations exist: perturbation of explanation-identified regions with observation of the prediction change (Theissler et al., 2022), area over the perturbation curve and ablation threshold measures for time series feature importance (Arsenault et al., 2025, p. 265:30) and surrogate fidelity computed as the error between surrogate and black-box outputs (Spinnato, 2023, pp. 38–39). Yet Arsenault et al. (2025, p. 265:30) conclude that few studies, if any, rigorously tested the faithfulness and the reliability of their explainability methods in financial time series forecasting and that the absence of quantitative interpretability metrics marks a domain-wide deficit.

The debate over attention weights as explanations crystallizes the faithfulness–plausibility distinction and bears directly on the transformer architectures included in this thesis. Attention is attractive because it is model-internal and temporally adaptive: weights are recomputed at each time step, allowing the model to track changing temporal relationships (Habiba et al., 2026, pp. 81–82). However, Arsenault et al. (2025, p. 265:18) summarize comparative studies finding that attention–based importance shows a low correlation with the one obtained from other methods, such as gradient-based and leave-one-out methods, concluding that if a reliable interpretation has to be plausible and faithful, then attention weights would not be reliable and that the reliability of attention depends on the context, the definition and the testing method.

Spinnato (2023, Chapter 4) adds a further distinction. Attention can be considered ante-hoc because its weights are calculated within the model. However, it can also be considered post-hoc because the resulting attention pattern may be an unintended by-product of model training. The methodological moral is that model internality is no guarantee of faithfulness an intrinsic explanation and a post-hoc explanation must both be tested not trusted by construction.

More broadly, the plausibility of an explanation is systematically easier to achieve and easier to display than its faithfulness and the reviewed literature repeatedly warns against conflating the two. Approximate attribution methods can misattribute or miss critical features in safety-critical settings (Kraft, 2025, p. 17), post-hoc techniques may not fully capture the complex interactions within deep models (Valsala Saratchandran, 2025, p. 309) and partial-dependence-style black-box measures obscure how architecture choices shape the interpretation itself (Dixon et al., 2020, p. 186). A broader problem underlies these findings: in interpretable machine learning, there is no clear ground truth against which an explanation can be checked (Molnar, 2022, p. 9). This makes it difficult to show that an explanation is correct rather than simply plausible or convincing.

Theissler (2024, para. 3.4) reports that user-based evaluations are avoided in the majority of XAI tool papers, so even plausibility is rarely measured. For financial forecasting, where an unfaithful but plausible attribution can misallocate capital or mask model failure, this gap between the two properties is precisely what RQ3’s faithfulness evaluation addresses.
Statistical Drivers versus Genuine Economic Drivers

The final strand of the review asks whether explanations, even faithful ones, identify economically meaningful structure. The baseline position of the empirical asset-pricing literature is restrictive: machine learning improves prediction, but predictive measurements do not by themselves identify economic mechanisms or equilibria and recovering mechanisms requires the researcher to add structure to build a hypothesized mechanism into the estimation problem (Gu et al., 2020, p. 2229). The interpretable-ML literature reaches the analogous conclusion from the other direction. Most interpretation methods describe the model rather than the real world and inferring real-world effects from them requires additional strong assumptions such as model unbiasedness (Molnar, 2022, pp. 28–29).

Both statements imply that a faithful attribution is, at best, evidence about the model’s mechanics, the step from model mechanics to economic drivers is a separate inferential act that the explanation method itself cannot legitimate.

Financial data make this step especially hazardous. Where the signal-to-noise ratio is low and multiple tests are run, spurious findings are mechanically generated (Bruce et al., 2020, pp. 112–115; López De Prado, 2020b, p. 106) and in-sample significance does not imply out-of-sample forecasting value (López De Prado, 2020b, p. 75). Asset-pricing theory adds another complication. Even when return predictability is real, it may reflect compensation for taking on risks that change over time, rather than a market inefficiency that investors can exploit (Cochrane, 2005, pp. 21–22). For example, an attribution method may identify a volatility indicator as predictive, but this pattern could reflect risk compensation, temporary mispricing or random noise. These three interpretations have very different economic meanings.

The causal-inference critique generalizes the point: predictive algorithms devoid of causal models can only fit a function to data, interpreting it through a model-blind lens (Gill, 2020, pp. 767–768). This thesis accordingly treats the alignment of attributions with economically interpretable signals as a separate validation dimension rather than as a by-product of predictive accuracy.

The literature also shows how economic plausibility can be assessed, although such checks remain imperfect. Gu et al. (2020, p. 2223) find that different machine-learning methods identify similar dominant predictive signals, including variations of momentum, liquidity, and volatility. These signal families can serve as an economically grounded reference for checking whether model attributions are plausible. Fischer and Krauss (2018, p. 654) attempt a direct post-hoc rationalization, distilling their LSTM’s behavior into a rules-based short-term reversal strategy, yet the distilled rules recover only about half of the network’s returns, indicating that the rationalization is incomplete and that a substantial share of the model’s logic resists economic redescription.

Green (2026, pp. 539–540) reports the related finding that local explanations of a deep calibration model do not align well with financial intuition, and von Zahn et al. (2025) show experimentally that explanations change users’ confidence and delegation behavior specifically when they reveal divergence between the model’s logic and the user’s own, a reminder that the practical value of an explanation lies precisely in exposing economically unexpected model behavior rather than in confirming prior beliefs. No reviewed study, however, systematically tests whether post-hoc attributions of stock-forecasting models capture these established economic drivers or instead track spurious, regime-specific correlations, this is the third gap addressed by RQ3.
Synthesis and Research Gaps

The reviewed literatures exhibit three points of broad agreement and three unresolved tensions. There is agreement, first, that flexible ML/DL models can outperform linear and random-walk benchmarks in equity prediction under favorable conditions (Fischer & Krauss, 2018; Gu et al., 2020), while the conditions themselves horizon, market, sample size, evaluation design moderate or even reverse the ranking (Mao et al., 2026; Molnar, 2022, pp. 57–58; Tsay, 2005, pp. 180–183). Second, there is agreement that reported gains require multiplicity-aware, leakage-free evaluation to be credible (Dixon et al., 2020, pp. 213–214; López De Prado, 2020b, pp. 105–124; Medeiros, 2022). Third, there is agreement that interpretability is institutionally necessary in finance and achievable through intrinsically interpretable models or post-hoc explanation methods(Arsenault et al., 2025; Biecek & Burzykowski, 2021, pp. 6–7; Hoang et al., 2026).

Against this consensus stand three tensions: whether the accuracy–interpretability trade-off is steep or negligible in practice (Section 3.2.1), whether attention and other model-internal signals constitute reliable explanations (Section 3.4.2) and whether predictive importance can ever be read as economic mechanism (Section 3.4.3). Each tension is asserted far more often than it is measured, and each is intensified not resolved by the temporal structure of financial data.

The thesis is positioned against the five closest works as follows. Arsenault et al. ((2025) survey XAI for financial time series forecasting and diagnose the fidelity and stability deficits, but as a survey they evaluate nothing experimentally, this thesis provides a bounded experimental response to that agenda while retaining important implementation limitations. Theissler et al. (2022) provide the faithfulness-evaluation protocols but for time series classification, this thesis transfers and adapts them to financial forecasting as a regression task with regime structure. Hu et al. (2026) deliver the financial forecasting benchmark with leakage control and regime-aware evaluation but no explainability track. This thesis evaluates explanation diagnostics alongside forecast metrics and uses one executed Monash-related Sunspot series as a limited cross-domain robustness block (Godahewa et al., 2021).

López de Prado (2020b) establishes the rigorous feature-importance program and the backtest-overfitting critique, but treats Shapley-based and surrogate explanations only in passing (p. 77) and does not examine temporal attribution stability, this thesis extends his program to the post-hoc toolbox and to the time dimension. Molnar (2022) provides the deepest methodological analysis of post-hoc interpretation. Its axioms, pitfalls, and limits under dependent features but is domain-agnostic, this thesis instantiates and stress-tests that analysis where its assumptions are most strained: on serially dependent, low-signal financial time series.

In sum, the literature demonstrates that accurate stock prediction with ML/DL is possible but fragile, that explanation methods exist in abundance, and that neither their stability, their faithfulness, nor their economic content has been established for financial time series forecasting. The three gaps are therefore not marginal omissions but direct consequences of how the constituent fields have developed. Financial ML optimized accuracy, XAI optimized plausibility, and time series evaluation optimized predictive rigor, with no subfield responsible for their intersection. The methodology of this thesis, presented in Chapter 4, is designed around precisely this intersection.

This chapter outlines the study's methodological framework, encompassing four financial market indices and the Monash Sunspot T1 benchmark dataset, two forecasting horizons, four lagged predictors, and seven model families. The evaluation employs rolling and expanding walk-forward validation schemes and examines three key dimensions: predictive accuracy, temporal stability, and explanation faithfulness.
Research Design

The study uses a comparative, retrospective experimental design. Model family, dataset, forecast horizon, and walk-forward scheme define the principal evaluation dimensions. The response variables are forecast error, directional agreement, R², attribution stability, and explanation-faithfulness diagnostics. Predictive and explanation outcomes inform RQ1, consecutive-fold and regime-stratified attributions inform RQ2 and additivity, intervention, cross-channel and native-model diagnostics inform RQ3.

The design has two complementary coverage layers. The native layer retains every executed fold: Linear Regression, ARIMA, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM have six folds per scheme with 252 test targets per full fold, while LSTM and TFT have four folds per scheme with 231 evaluated targets. The primary comparative layer uses the intersection of forecast origins across all seven models. For rolling evaluation, static folds 2–5 align with deep folds 0–3, for expanding evaluation, static and deep folds 0–3 align directly. Within each block the deep origin range begins at test start plus 21. The intersection therefore contains four blocks of 231 origins, or 924 origins for every series–horizon scheme.

Replication takes three forms. First, rolling and expanding windows provide repeated temporal evaluations and function as related robustness tracks, not as independent replications. Second, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM average predictions from seeds 20261017 and 20261018. Their explanations are averaged over the same two constituents and per-probe cross-seed agreement is exported. Third, the same configuration is applied to four financial indices and the Sunspot benchmark. Linear Regression, ARIMA, LSTM, and TFT use one seed, consequently, stochastic uncertainty is not estimated symmetrically across all model families.

The unit of aggregation is distinguished from the unit of observation. Native fold metrics are calculated within each fold. Primary matched metrics are calculated from all 924 shared origins, with matched-fold metrics retained for inspection. Diebold–Mariano tests use observation-level squared errors rather than a constant fold-level RMSE². Explanation-stability counts refer to probe–fold-pair rows, while faithfulness success fractions refer to explained folds. These levels are not pooled into one significance test or one composite “trustworthiness” score.

Figure 1. provides an overview of the complete experimental pipeline. Input datasets are frozen before model development, and raw-row identifiers are preserved throughout lag construction. Each model-specific notebook exports observation-level predictions and supporting explanation evidence. Finally, a synthesis procedure identifies the intersection of common forecast origins across models before conducting statistical comparisons.

Temporal Preprocessing and Feature Engineering
Lag Construction and Modeling Frames

Every tabular model receives four predictors: lag_1, lag_5, lag_21, and lag_252. For financial series, each predictor is a lagged log return, xt,l=rt-l. For Sunspot, each is a lagged native value, xt,l=vt-l. For the financial data, these lags capture values from the previous trading session and from approximately one week, one month, and one year earlier. However, the thesis uses them only as predictive inputs, not as evidence of separate economic mechanisms.

The frame function constructs all lags and both targets before trimming the largest lag and target horizon and dropping remaining missing values. A source_row identifier is attached before trimming. It maps every frame row back to the original return or native-value series and is used to repair ARIMA alignment and to verify every exported target date. No rolling volatility, momentum, drawdown, macroeconomic, liquidity, or other exogenous variables are added.

Linear, tree, and deep tabular features are standardized using statistics fitted on the training portion of each fold. The same fitted scaler is applied to test and explanation inputs. ARIMA remains univariate and does not use the four-lag predictor vector, its native selected-lag counterfactuals are defined separately below.
Walk-Forward Splits and Validation Tails

The common nominal settings are a minimum training window of 500 observations, a test span of 252, purge 5, embargo 5, and rolling and expanding schemes. Both schemes are established approaches to temporal forecast evaluation (Ballarin, 2024; Medeiros, 2022, pp. 111–120). For a frame of length n, rolling fold k starts its test block at n-K×252+k×252. Expanding fold k starts at 500+5+5+k×252. Training ends ten observations before the test start. Rolling training retains at most the most recent 500 observations before that gap, expanding training starts at the beginning of the frame.

The implementation subtracts purge plus embargo before the test block. Operationally, this creates a ten-observation pre-test gap, it does not implement a separate post-test embargo. At each ARIMA forecast origin, the state is updated with every newly observed raw value through that origin, including observations in the pre-test gap. Parameter estimates remain fixed within the fold, while the state uses only information available at the origin.

Static models use K=6 and deep models K=4. Deep inputs contain 21 consecutive frame rows immediately before each target origin. The evaluated native deep origins therefore run from test_start + 21 through test_end - 1, yielding 231 targets in a complete block. Test sequences may include history immediately preceding the test block, which is available at the forecast origin, they never include future target values.

Boosted trees and neural networks use the final 10% of training rows or sequences for early stopping, with a minimum of 50. There is no additional purge between the fitting and early-stopping partitions. Models are not refit on the validation tail after the stopping point is selected. Neural networks restore the best validation state, and boosted trees retain their early-stopped fit.

Linear Regression and ARIMA

Linear Regression estimates an ordinary least-squares mapping from the four standardized lag variables to the target. If βj is the fitted coefficient and ztj is a standardized predictor, the attribution ztjβj is exact up to numerical precision. The baseline includes the intercept and the training-mean feature contribution. Prediction, attribution sum and baseline are compared directly for every explained probe.

ARIMA selects by AIC among 1,0,0, 2,0,0, 1,0,1, 2,0,1, 3,0,0, 1,1,0, and 2,1,0. For financial data, the h forecasts from an origin are summed to predict the cumulative log return, for Sunspot, the h-th native-value forecast is used. The selected model is fitted on the raw observations corresponding to the actual training frame, not on lag-trimmed positions applied to an untrimmed array. Its state uses the univariate observation through the current origin. Common-origin matching therefore aligns targets and dates across models, but it does not make ARIMA’s information set identical to the four-lag tabular predictor vector.

ARIMA does not have four tabular predictors, so SHAP, PFI, LIME, and the generic deletion/insertion implementation are not imputed for it. Instead, its native explanation measures how the forecast changes when each of four historical observations at lags 1, 5, 21, and 252 is replaced by the training mean while model parameters remain fixed. Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM

Random Forest uses 100 trees per seed, maximum depth 10, and minimum leaf size 20. XGBoost and LightGBM use at most 200 rounds, depth 6, learning rate 0.05, row and column sampling 0.8, L1 regularization 0.1, L2 regularization 1.0, and 25-round early stopping. The two boosted models use the preserved validation tail. All tree forecasts average the two seed-specific predictions.

The explained predictor is the same two-seed ensemble. For each constituent s, TreeSHAP produces feature attributions ϕtjs and an expected value bs. Because the ensemble prediction and TreeSHAP decomposition are linear in the constituent models, the full-ensemble explanation is

The additivity residual is computed against the averaged constituent predictions not against one arbitrarily selected seed. Constituent attributions are also compared per probe to measure seed sensitivity.
LSTM and Simplified TFT

The LSTM has two recurrent layers, hidden size 64, dropout 0.1, and a linear output from the final hidden state. The simplified TFT applies a variable-selection softmax to time-averaged inputs, multiplies the sequence by the resulting four weights, encodes it with an LSTM, applies four-head self-attention, and produces a linear output from the final attended position. Both networks use a lookback window of 21 observations, a maximum of 25 training epochs, a batch size of 64, the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001, and early stopping with a patience of 8 epochs. Training is limited to one CPU thread to keep resource use consistent, and no GPU is used.

For each explanation probe at frame position t, the input is constructed from the contiguous interval [t-21,t). This corrects the earlier practice of selecting spaced probe rows and then constructing artificial sequences from those rows. KernelSHAP uses 40 training-sequence backgrounds and 100 coalition samples per explained instance. The flattened 84 coordinates are interpreted as 21time positions by four lag channels. It allows opposing contributions within a channel to cancel out, unlike the earlier sign-by-absolute-sum transformation, which removed this information. For TFT, mean variable-selection weights and attention recency are retained as native signals, but attention is not presumed to be a faithful explanation.
Explainability Diagnostics
Attribution Channels and Common Probe Origins

The explanation methods are deliberately model-appropriate. Linear Regression and ARIMA have native mechanistic channels, tree ensembles have exact TreeSHAP decompositions up to numerical approximation, LSTM and TFT have approximate post-hoc KernelSHAP. For every series, horizon, and scheme, the probe span begins at the deep-compatible origin range of the last explained test block and continues through the end of the modeling frame. Probe positions are drawn evenly across that span. The same positions are used for every explained fold of that model, and each position is out-of-sample with respect to every explained fitted model. Extending beyond a single test block prevents a quiet final block from removing crisis-stratum evidence by construction. Static models explain four folds with 40 probes, deep models explain three folds with 30 probes. ARIMA uses the static coverage and all 80 explanation units. The static and deep groups have different spans and probe counts, so their explanation summaries are not an origin-matched seven-model panel, origin matching is used for the predictive comparison and for consecutive folds within each model.

Attribution exports include model, method, series, horizon, scheme, fold, probe, origin index, origin and target dates, regime stratum, feature. Raw magnitudes are not compared directly across targets or explanation methods. For cross-model feature displays, absolute attributions are normalized within each probe by their sum across the four features.

Faithfulness and Cross-Channel Diagnostics

For Linear Regression, the tree models, LSTM and TFT, mean absolute attribution supplies a four-feature ranking. Permutation-feature importance is computed on the explained observations. For deep models, an entire lag channel is permuted across samples while each sequence’s internal temporal order remains intact. The Spearman correlation between permutation importance and attribution magnitude is reported as cross-diagnostic agreement, not as independent proof of truth.

Deletion and insertion use the same four lag groups for model-ranked and random orderings. In a static model a deleted feature is set to its standardized training-mean value of zero. In a deep model, all 21 positions of the selected lag channel are set to zero. Thirty-two random permutations of the same four groups provide controls. A faithful deletion ranking should increase loss more quickly than the random mean, a faithful insertion ranking should reduce loss more quickly. Area under the five-point curve is normalized by four intervals. These are zero-baseline intervention diagnostics and may produce off-manifold sequences.

A weighted local ridge surrogate supplies a secondary LIME-style diagnostic. The calculation uses the first 20 ordered probes in each explanation unit, or all probes when fewer than 20 are available. For each selected probe, 300 synthetic samples are drawn from a standard-normal distribution in the standardized feature space. The first 200 samples are used to fit a ridge surrogate with regularization 10-8 and the remaining 100 form a holdout set. The samples are therefore not drawn directly around the probe. Instead, proximity to the probe enters through the kernel weight

It should therefore be read as error over the synthetic holdout region, not as a purely local, kernel-weighted fidelity measure. Mean absolute surrogate coefficients are aggregated to the four lag channels and compared with attribution importance through Spearman correlation. The first-20-probe restriction, global sampling, and unweighted holdout score limit the diagnostic’s local interpretation. It is reported as a secondary comparison, and no execution of an external LIME library is claimed. For TFT, native variable-selection weights are additionally correlated with KernelSHAP importance. Regime-Shift Analysis

Financial regime labels are retained as ex post descriptive strata. They use 63 session rolling return means and standard deviations, with full-series quantiles defining bull, bear, boundary, and crisis categories. As they are based on full-series quantiles, they cannot serve as real-time trading signals. Regime robustness is therefore assessed by comparing explanation stability across regimes and examining consistency between rolling and expanding validation schemes.
Reproducibility and Experimental Setup

The final notebooks are standalone and contain their common execution code. Each notebook verifies the frozen inputs, completes all planned forecast and explanation units, exports evidence, reads the artifacts back, and checks output hashes. The execution environment is macOS with Python 3.12 and CPU-only computation.

The methodological records include observation-level data exports, common-origin alignment, block-aware Diebold–Mariano (DM) testing, raw-row ARIMA mapping, contiguous deep-learning probes, full-ensemble TreeSHAP, net neural SHAP aggregation, actual additivity residuals, and equal four-group controls. These corrections aim to improve the validity and reliability of the experimental results while preserving the seven model families, datasets and indices, forecasting targets, four lag features, outer validation splits, random seeds, and network architectures. Replacing the Monash source file with the original raw data also ensures data traceability without changing the Sunspot time series or its observation dates.

The cross-model analysis is conducted only after all seven models have successfully passed their completion audits. The reproducibility evidence confirms the consistency of computational procedures and experimental outputs.
