RQ1: Accuracy, Interpretability and the Post-hoc Trade-off

RQ1 asks to what extent SHAP-or LIME-style post-hoc methods reduce the accuracy–interpretability trade-off between intrinsically interpretable models and black-box architectures. The predictive results show no uniform trade-off in either direction. LightGBM has the lowest mean relative RMSE and XGBoost is second. Boosted-tree approaches can therefore remain competitive with simpler models when suitable explanation methods are available. However, neither beats persistence on average, and ARIMA has the best mean rank. Linear Regression combines exact structural attributions with nine significant financial pairwise wins and no significant losses. These findings do not support the assumption that more complex black-box models usually produce more accurate forecasts.

The deep architectures provide further evidence against a universal advantage of complex models. TFT wins selected rolling comparisons and LSTM is best in one financial cell, but LSTM also has nine significant losses and no significant financial wins. Random Forest has the weakest mean rank and 15 significant losses, even though TreeSHAP makes its predictor easy to decompose. Both simple extremes are therefore rejected: black-box models are not consistently superior and intrinsically interpretable models are not automatically best. Performance depends on the index, horizon, training-window scheme, and model specification.

The additional benchmark tests, which use each model’s full forecast coverage, strengthen this conclusion without changing the main experimental design. Across 224 financial model benchmark tests, no pipeline significantly improves on persistence or the training mean after cell-wide BH adjustment. Indeed, none of the comparisons in which a model has lower loss than the benchmark reaches even the unadjusted p<0.05 threshold. After the fold-block-aware adjustment across 14 tests, 26 comparisons show that a model performs significantly worse than the benchmark. The less conservative two-test sensitivity analysis produces 39 such losses and still finds no significant model wins. Because these tests retain unequal native origins, they cannot be used to rank model power or reverse the matched-origin comparison. They do, however, remove the concern that descriptive persistence gains were simply hidden by restricting attention to pairwise model tests.

Post-hoc methods reduce the trade-off in a narrower practical sense. TreeSHAP gives RF, XGBoost, and LightGBM a coherent decomposition of the complete two-seed predictor, while KernelSHAP provides a common lag-channel summary for LSTM and TFT. This makes model behavior easier to inspect without replacing the nonlinear model with a linear model for every purpose. The local ridge surrogate and permutation importance add secondary views. Post-hoc explanation therefore reduces the opacity cost of keeping a nonlinear predictor.

That reduction in opacity is not equivalent to an accuracy gain, a faithful economic explanation, or temporal reliability. The accuracy comparison is determined by the fitted predictors, not by applying SHAP after fitting. Post-hoc methods cannot retroactively improve RMSE. They can only change the evidence available to a user, and the RQ2 and RQ3 diagnostics show that this evidence has its own failure modes. The most defensible RQ1 conclusion is therefore partial and conditional mitigation: post-hoc XAI broadens the set of models whose forecasts can be inspected, but the executed study finds no general accuracy–interpretability trade-off for it to overcome and no basis for recommending a black-box pipeline solely on expected predictive superiority.

The Sunspot block prevents overgeneralizing this conclusion. ARIMA leads at one session, while Linear Regression and LSTM lead in different five-session schemes. The rolling five-session gains of LSTM and TFT show that nonlinear architectures can be useful on a series with different temporal structure. Their failure to reproduce the same advantage under expanding evaluation or across financial cells also shows why architecture-wide claims require more than one favorable benchmark.

Finally, the analysis compares complete modeling approaches rather than testing model architectures in isolation. ARIMA updates a univariate state, static tabular models receive four lag features, and neural models receive 21-row sequences. Common origins remove unequal evaluation coverage but do not equalize those information sets. This is not a defect in the matched analysis, it is a boundary on what the comparison identifies. The results show which complete forecasting approach performs better on the same prediction targets. They do not show which model architecture would perform best if all models used identical inputs, were tuned to the same extent, and were evaluated over the same number of repeated random-seed runs.
RQ2: Temporal Stability, Non-stationarity and Regime Robustness

RQ2 asks whether feature attributions remain temporally stable and robust to non-stationarity, structural breaks and regime shifts. The executed evidence supports a model- and channel-specific answer: stability varies considerably and no model establishes universal robustness across all temporal and regime diagnostics. Consecutive-fold Spearman correlation, cosine similarity, and top-feature agreement capture different aspects of stability. They sometimes agree on broad model differences but do not justify a single stability ranking at every probe. Cross-model comparisons are also less strongly identified than within-model consecutive-fold comparisons because static and deep models use different explanation spans and probe counts.

Overall median correlations range from 1.000000 for ARIMA to 0.200000 for TFT, but ARIMA’s tenth percentile remains −1.000000. The most consistent temporal result is the training-window contrast: all seven models have higher expanding than rolling window stability and TFT’s rolling median falls to 0.000000. This suggests that restricting estimation to 500 recent observations affects not only forecast errors but also the repeatability of model-mechanistic attributions. It does not establish that longer windows are always preferable. Expanding estimation can retain obsolete regimes, both tracks share the same underlying history, and their explanation spans differ. The rolling/expanding contrast may therefore reflect probe placement as well as training history.

The wider common probe span is important for this answer. Restricting explanations to one final test block removed crisis-labelled observations for both deep models, which would have made a regime conclusion an artifact of probe placement. Extending the span through the modeling-frame end retains out-of-sample status relative to every explained fitted model and restores regime diversity. This change affects explanation evidence only, it does not alter the matched forecast origins or predictive rankings.

Three distinctions are necessary when interpreting Table 11. and Figure 6. First, a high median rank correlation does not imply large economic effects or accurate forecasts. A model can preserve the ordering of four nearly zero contributions. Second, a change in the top feature does not necessarily imply a large change in prediction, especially when relative shares are close to uniform. Third, rank correlation over only four features gives a coarse measure. The median can hide negative tails and disagreement at individual probes. For this reason, the tenth percentiles, cosine values, top-feature rates, and sample counts are essential parts of the result.

The regime contrasts do not justify the simple hypothesis that every explanation deteriorates in a bear or crisis stratum. Differences relative to the boundary stratum vary in sign and magnitude by model. In some channels a high median persists across strata, in others, crisis or bull observations differ from boundary observations but are supported by few rows. Rolling and expanding tracks also need not agree, because they fit models on different amounts of history. The results do not mean that market regimes are unimportant. They simply show that explanations do not always become less stable in the same regimes.

Tree seed stability answers a different question from fold stability. Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM explain the average of two seeds and their constituent attributions can be compared directly. High seed-level agreement would show that the chosen pair leads to similar model mechanics at a probe, it would not show that the fitted mechanism remains unchanged as the training window moves. Conversely, lower seed agreement identifies stochastic sensitivity even when a consecutive-fold median is high. Only two seeds were tested and the neural models were not evaluated with repeated seeds. These results therefore provide a limited check of variability, not a complete picture of uncertainty.

The answer to RQ2 is consequently limited and conditional temporal robustness. The study measures stability across consecutive fitted models at common probes and across preserved ex post regime strata. It does not identify historical structural-break dates, estimate real-time regime transitions or prove stability under future distribution shifts. Under these regime definitions, the results show differences between models and explanation channels, as well as variation in groups with few observations. The evidence does not support a general claim that explanations are either robust or fragile.
RQ3: Faithfulness to Model Mechanics
Additivity Is Supported, but It Is Only the First Test

The first question about how the model works is whether the attribution values can reproduce the model’s own prediction. The exact linear contributions, native ARIMA counterfactuals, and full-ensemble tree decompositions satisfy this condition up to very small floating-point or approximation residuals. LSTM and TFT KernelSHAP residuals are also small, although they are approximation results rather than algebraic identities. The largest XGBoost and neural residuals occur on the raw Sunspot scale, financial maxima are below 3.3×10-9, 3.0×10-8 and 2.3×10-8 for XGBoost, LSTM, and TFT, respectively. XGBoost’s maximum residual is small but not exactly zero and is reported as such.

These results correct a common interpretation error: additivity is not established by merely calling a vector “SHAP” The calculation compares the sum of attribution coordinates and expected value with the prediction from the same explained ensemble or network. For the neural models, the sum is taken over all 84 flattened coordinates before aggregation into four lag channels. For tree ensembles, both seed-specific attributions and expected values are averaged and the residual is measured against the averaged prediction. The decomposition therefore refers to the model that actually generates the exported forecast.

Nevertheless, additivity demonstrates internal numerical consistency only. It does not establish that the chosen background represents a meaningful counterfactual, that a lag channel is economically important, or that the model learned a transferable mechanism. An explanation that adds up perfectly to an overfitted model’s prediction is still explaining an overfitted model. Additivity does not correct the overfitting.
Intervention and Cross-channel Results Are Mixed

The deletion/insertion results provide a separate behavioral test. A model-ranked deletion should be more damaging than the mean of 32 random orderings and a model-ranked insertion should be more helpful. The observed success fractions are neither universal success nor universal failure. Tree models generally perform better than the neural models under these diagnostics but the rates vary by model and unit. LSTM and TFT outcomes near one half indicate that model-ranked interventions frequently fail to beat the random control. These failures prevent a blanket claim that SHAP rankings identify the most behaviorally important lag groups under zero-baseline intervention.

Across model families, PFI and SHAP often have median rank correlations close to zero, while SHAP and the LIME-style surrogate often correlate strongly. This difference should not be treated as a problem that can be solved by choosing the method with the more favorable result. PFI measures the effect of disrupting a feature channel on realized loss. The surrogate measures whether a distance-weighted linear approximation reproduces predictions and importance rankings on globally generated synthetic samples, using the first 20 probes per unit. They ask different questions and can give different answers when features are dependent, predictions are nonlinear or perturbations move away from the data manifold. The surrogate’s unweighted holdout MSE and restricted probe coverage further limit its interpretation as a local fidelity score.

TFT native variable-selection weights add another diagnostic rather than ground truth. Their agreement with KernelSHAP is imperfect and financial attention-recency values near ten are close to the mean position of a uniform distribution over 21 sequence positions. This does not support interpreting attention as a consistent recency explanation. Sunspot attention is more recency-weighted but that domain difference still does not make attention a faithful causal measure. ARIMA’s native selected-lag contributions are more directly tied to model mechanics, yet their meaning remains constrained by the small candidate set and univariate information structure.

For RQ3, the results support numerical additivity but give mixed evidence of broader faithfulness. The implemented decompositions reproduce the models’ predictions with only small numerical errors. Intervention and cross-channel results are less consistent and native and post-hoc signals are not interchangeable. No single diagnostic establishes every aspect of faithfulness. Strong performance on one diagnostic cannot cancel contradictory evidence from another.
RQ3: Genuine Economic Drivers Versus Statistical Associations

The question of economic drivers needs a different answer: this study cannot show whether the highlighted features actually cause economic changes. The models contain only lagged prices for financial indices or native lagged Sunspot values. An attribution to lag_1, lag_5, lag_21, or lag_252 describes how a fitted pipeline uses a past input. By itself, it cannot identify monetary policy, earnings expectations, liquidity, risk premia, investor sentiment, or another causal economic mechanism.

This limitation is not repaired by high additivity, stable rankings, or agreement between SHAP and a surrogate. Those results can establish that a model uses a variable consistently. They cannot establish why the variable predicts, whether it proxies for an omitted economic factor or whether intervening on the proposed economic mechanism would change the market outcome. The near-uniform average relative shares for several models further discourage a simple story in which one lag represents a stable economic driver. ARIMA’s stronger concentration on the first selected lag is a property of its fitted autoregressive mechanics, not proof of a one-day economic force.

Spurious association remains possible for several reasons: weak low-order signal, omitted common factors, regime-dependent relationships, overlapping targets, overfitting, and mechanical dependence among lagged prices. Conversely, the analysis does not prove that every lag association is spurious. It establishes that the design cannot distinguish genuine economic causation from predictive association. The results do not show that the drivers are spurious, but this design also cannot confirm that they represent real economic causes. Testing them would require exogenous economic variables, explicit identification assumptions, event or natural-experiment designs, economic theory, and out-of-sample validation of the proposed mechanism.

Implications for Trustworthy Financial Forecasting

The results support a practical evaluation sequence. First, establish whether a forecast improves on a transparent benchmark at identical origins. Second, test whether the explanation reconstructs the actual predictor rather than a different seed, model, or surrogate. Third, examine stability across training windows and stochastic fits. Fourth, use behavioral interventions and alternative diagnostics to look for disagreement. Finally, state separately whether the variables and design can support economic or human decision claims. A failure at a later stage cannot be repaired by success at an earlier one.

This sequence refines the accuracy–interpretability discussion in the covered literature. The relevant choice is not simply “linear and understandable” versus “deep and accurate” In this experiment, simpler pipelines are often competitive, while post-hoc methods expose both useful decompositions and unresolved instability. Trustworthiness is therefore multidimensional and sometimes internally conflicting.

For practitioners, the main recommendation is to use these explanations cautiously. A SHAP summary can show which lagged inputs a fitted model relies on, but without further evidence it should not be treated as a basis for investment decisions or as an explanation of what causes market movements. Forecasts with negative average R² and no average persistence gain should not be deployed as though moderate directional accuracy implied profitability. Explanation plots should be accompanied by their probe coverage, model version, background data, residuals, intervention comparisons, and regime counts.

Future research should repeat the neural-model experiments with different seeds, add economic predictors without data leakage, use independently dated crises and structural breaks, and test whether the explanations are robust and useful for human decisions. These extensions would address the remaining research questions rather than simply increase model complexity.

These interpretations provide useful insights but do not make the simplified forecasting framework a comprehensive model of financial markets. The following limitations therefore define the scope of the research findings rather than representing unresolved computational issues.
Data-Related Limitations
Sample Composition and Market Coverage

The financial evidence concerns four large daily equity indices: S&P 500, DAX, NASDAQ Composite, and DJIA. Three are United States indices, and their constituent overlap and shared global risk factors limit cross-series independence. The DAX adds a non-US market, but one additional index does not establish global generalizability. Individual equities, small-cap markets, emerging markets, fixed income, commodities, foreign exchange, cryptocurrencies, and alternative forecast frequencies remain outside the experiment. Results should consequently be read as evidence for these index series and periods, not as a universal property of financial forecasting.

The sample ends in December 2025 for the financial inputs and May 2020 for Sunspot. Walk-forward evaluation reduces temporal leakage in model fitting, but it does not make the study a prospective live forecasting exercise. Data revisions, index-composition changes, market microstructure, and execution constraints are not modeled. Adjusted closing prices are appropriate for the defined return calculation, yet they do not represent a directly tradable instrument with bid–ask spreads and transaction costs.
Restricted Feature Set and Target Definition

The four predictors are lagged values at 1, 5, 21, and 252 observations. They omit prices relative to moving averages, realized and implied volatility, volume, liquidity, earnings, valuation ratios, interest rates, exchange rates, macroeconomic releases, news, and sentiment. This restriction preserves the study’s scope and makes model comparison tractable, but it severely limits economic interpretation. A high attribution to lag_21, for example, identifies reliance on a particular lagged input, it does not reveal a monthly macroeconomic mechanism.

The financial target is a cumulative future log return at one and five sessions. It is not a price-level forecast, risk-adjusted portfolio return, probability of a price increase, or trading rule. Directional accuracy treats sign agreement literally and ignores magnitude, costs, and economic significance. The five-session targets overlap, so directional hits and errors are temporally dependent. The Sunspot target is a native future value, and its error scale is not comparable to financial log returns.
Sunspot Provenance and Benchmark Role

Sunspot activity serves only as a non-financial robustness benchmark. Its generating process, observational properties, and seasonal structure differ from those of equity indices. Strong or weak performance on Sunspot cannot validate financial market predictability and explanation stability on Sunspot cannot establish financial explanation robustness. Its role is to reveal whether model-specific behavior is confined to one domain.
Methodological Limitations
Temporal Splits and Inner Validation

The outer split leaves a ten-observation gap before the test set: five purge observations and five embargo observations. For early stopping, the boosted-tree and neural models use the last 10% of the training data for validation, with no additional purge between the training and validation sets. Adjacent training and validation targets can therefore overlap, especially at the five-session horizon. Models are not refit on the validation tail after early stopping. These choices may affect stopping points and effective training coverage.

Rolling training uses at most 500 observations, which is compact relative to the multi-decade sample and may limit the estimation of slowly changing relationships. Expanding training uses more history but can retain observations from structurally different periods. Neither scheme is uniformly superior, their divergence is evidence about sensitivity to training-window design. They share data and origins and must not be counted as independent replications.
Statistical Inference and Stochastic Replication

The Diebold–Mariano tests use observation-level squared errors and HAC lag h-1, with autocovariances restricted to contiguous matched blocks. This addresses the loss defect and the overlap implied by the target horizon. It does not solve every small-sample or serial-dependence problem. The asymptotic normal reference distribution can be approximate in finite samples and folding schemes leave only four matched blocks per cell. Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment is applied within each 21-pair family at q=0.05, not across all 420 pairwise tests simultaneously. Results are therefore family-wise evidence within each cell, not a global probability that a model is universally best.

Two-seed averaging is available only for the tree models. Linear Regression and ARIMA are deterministic conditional on their implementation but LSTM and TFT use one seed and can exhibit materially different training outcomes under another initialization or data order. Tree seed-attribution agreement does not estimate neural stochastic instability.
Explainability-Related Limitations
Explanation Coverage and Probe Dependence

Static explanation units cover four folds per scheme with 40 probes and deep units cover three folds with 30 probes. These are structured evaluation samples not a census of all forecast origins. Probe positions are evenly spaced from the last explained test block to the end of the data frame and are reused across consecutive folds. This reuse is necessary to compare stability at the same positions. However, the limited number of probes restricts coverage over time, and some series–scheme groups still contain only a few probes. The extended positions are explanation-only origins: no predictive performance claim is based on forecasts beyond each fold’s designated test block. Explanation summaries can be sensitive to the span and to the number and placement of probes.

Different models have different explanation channels and coverage. ARIMA native counterfactuals are not SHAP values, TFT variable-selection weights are not interchangeable with KernelSHAP, and the LIME-style surrogate is not an external LIME-package output. Cross-model comparisons consequently emphasize common constructs rank agreement, cosine similarity, top-feature agreement, and within-probe relative magnitude without claiming that all values share identical semantics.
Narrow Stability and Regime Constructs

Consecutive-fold Spearman correlation measures the order of four attribution values. With only four features, the coefficient occupies coarse discrete levels, so reported medians should not be read as high-precision continuous measurements. Correlation can be high when all attributions are negligible and it can be unstable when their ordering changes despite similar forecast behavior. Cosine similarity adds directional geometry and top feature agreement captures only the dominant feature. None measures prediction stability, calibration or economic stability directly. Undefined correlations and zero-norm cosines remain missing, so summary counts must accompany medians.

The financial regimes are descriptive groups based on 63-session rolling statistics and quantiles calculated from the full sample. They do not represent independently dated recessions, crises, or structural breaks. The crisis label denotes high estimated volatility within the sample, not a verified historical crisis such as a specific crash. Full-series quantiles also use future distributional information for descriptive labeling. Consequently, RQ2 receives an answer about temporal and regime-stratified robustness under this operationalization, not a definitive test of every form of non-stationarity or structural change.
Faithfulness Diagnostics Are Not Interchangeable

Additivity is necessary for a SHAP-style decomposition but insufficient for economic or causal validity. Exact linear, native ARIMA and tree-ensemble residuals demonstrate numerical consistency with their respective predictors. KernelSHAP residuals measure the approximation actually returned by the explainer, but small residuals do not validate the background distribution, coalition sampling assumptions or lag aggregation as a complete temporal explanation.

Permutation importance, deletion/insertion tests, and local surrogate fidelity can disagree because they assess different aspects of the model. Zero-baseline deletion replaces feature values with standardized training means, which may create unrealistic return sequences. Permuting a lag channel preserves within-sequence order but can break cross-feature dependence. The surrogate has three further restrictions: it uses only the first 20 ordered probes per explanation unit, draws samples globally from a standard-normal distribution in standardized feature space and reports an unweighted holdout MSE. Its samples can leave the natural data manifold and its fidelity score is not a purely local weighted error. Agreement with SHAP is therefore diagnostic convergence, not independent ground truth. A failed intervention comparison likewise identifies a failure under that intervention definition, not a global verdict on every possible explanation method.
Native Signals and Seed Sensitivity

Tree-model comparisons use only two seeds. They show whether this pair produces similar four-feature rankings at the same probes, but not how results vary across a wider range of seeds. LSTM and TFT were not tested with repeated seeds or repeated KernelSHAP samples on fixed models. Their fold-to-fold stability may therefore combine the effects of model retraining and explanation sampling, which this design cannot separate. The three types of stability across folds, across seeds, and across explanation samples are distinct measures.
Economic, Human, and External Validity

The most important identification limitation is unchanged by computational correction: lagged prices and native Sunspot values do not identify genuine causal economic drivers. Attributions may reflect autocorrelation, volatility states, mechanical index behavior, proxy relationships, overfitting or robust predictive regularities. The available variables cannot distinguish these possibilities from monetary policy, earnings expectations, risk premia, liquidity, or investor behavior. The thesis therefore does not claim to have identified genuine economic drivers, feature names alone are not economic explanations. No domain experts or end users assessed whether the explanations were understandable, useful, or actionable, and the study includes no human-participant research, decision-quality test, or regulatory compliance certification. Faithfulness and stability are computational properties and do not establish transparency for practitioners. The study also does not evaluate investment performance using portfolio optimization, position sizing, transaction costs, or risk limits. Directional accuracy above 50% alone does not demonstrate profitability.

This thesis examined whether explainable machine learning can make financial time series forecasting more trustworthy. Accuracy, interpretability, stability, faithfulness, and economic meaning were evaluated separately because success in one area does not guarantee success in another.

The final study evaluates Linear Regression, ARIMA, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, LSTM, and a simplified Temporal Fusion Transformer on four financial indices and the Monash Sunspot benchmark. It defines the prediction targets, four lagged predictors, walk-forward schemes, model families, random seeds, and training limits. The supporting evidence includes observation-level predictions, shared forecast origins, ARIMA updates on raw data rows, supervised-target benchmarks, TreeSHAP for the full ensemble, uninterrupted neural input histories, equivalent intervention controls, and pairwise tests that account for forecast blocks.

The answer to RQ1 is that post-hoc XAI reduces the accuracy–interpretability trade-off only to a limited extent and under certain conditions. It makes nonlinear models easier to inspect, but it does not improve their predictive performance, and black-box models show no general accuracy advantage. No model outperforms persistence on average across the financial cells. LightGBM achieves the lowest mean relative RMSE, ARIMA the best mean rank, and Linear Regression the strongest financial pairwise significance profile. Deep models win selected cells but also record substantial losses. The supplementary native-coverage analysis reinforces this limitation: none of the 224 financial model–benchmark tests show a significant model win under either correction approach. Simpler models therefore remain credible forecasting candidates. Choosing a black-box model requires predictive evidence for the particular forecasting setting, not an assumption that greater complexity improves performance.

The answer to RQ2 is that temporal and regime robustness are model- and diagnostic-dependent. Consecutive-fold rank correlation, cosine similarity, and top-feature agreement reveal heterogeneous stability rather than a universal pattern. Expanding-window attributions are more stable than rolling-window attributions for all seven models, although high medians can conceal severe adverse tails. Regime contrasts do not establish a common bear- or crisis-regime degradation effect, and sparse strata limit stronger conclusions. Tree seed agreement provides additional evidence about stochastic sensitivity but is not interchangeable with temporal stability. These answers apply to the preserved ex post regime operationalization and structured probe coverage, not to independently dated structural breaks or every future form of non-stationarity.

For the mechanistic part of RQ3, numerical additivity is supported, but broader faithfulness is mixed. The implemented attributions reconstruct their respective model outputs up to small residuals, and native ARIMA counterfactuals provide model-specific mechanistic evidence. The results of deletion/insertion and permutation tests are mixed. Surrogate methods often show stronger agreement than PFI, but this comparison must be interpreted with the surrogate’s global sampling and limited probe coverage in mind. TFT’s native signals should also not be treated as equivalent to KernelSHAP. Additivity therefore provides useful evidence about a decomposition, but it cannot by itself prove faithfulness.

For the economic part of RQ3, the study design cannot identify genuine causal drivers. Lagged price and native Sunspot attributions cannot reliably distinguish economic mechanisms from predictive or spurious associations. The thesis does not claim that all observed associations are spurious. Instead, it shows that the available variables and study design cannot distinguish between these possibilities.

The thesis therefore does not present any model or XAI method as inherently trustworthy. Its contribution is a reproducible empirical evaluation that separates trustworthiness into distinct, testable components. Predictive skill is assessed against benchmarks at common forecast origins, explanations are examined in relation to the actual fitted predictor, and stability across folds, seeds, and explanation samples is treated as three distinct properties. Disagreements in intervention tests and across explanation channels are reported explicitly, while economic interpretations remain bounded by the identification design. Accordingly, lag-based attributions are not interpreted as evidence of causal economic drivers, and neither predictive performance nor additivity alone is sufficient to establish trustworthiness. The findings support cautious, setting-specific model inspection rather than universal claims of predictive superiority or explanation reliability.

Future research should retrain the neural models across multiple seeds, incorporate a broader set of economic predictors without introducing data leakage, evaluate independently dated crises and structural breaks, test additional counterfactuals that remain on the temporal data manifold, and examine whether explanations improve expert decision-making. More complex model architectures alone would not address the study’s principal limitations. Further progress requires stronger causal identification, replicated uncertainty analyses, and explanation evaluations that transparently report negative and conflicting evidence.
The thesis therefore concludes that, within its experimental scope, explainable machine learning is a useful tool for model inspection but cannot guarantee trustworthy financial forecasting.
